html: Write the number 18 475 correct to the nearest thousand.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 18 000 — B1, cao, and nothing else scores. The two thousands either side are 18 000 and 19 000, with the halfway point at 18 500; 18 475 sits below it, so it rounds down. The one digit that decides it is the hundreds digit, 4 — once that is below 5 the 7 and the 5 behind it play no part at all. The slip to name is reading “475, nearly 500” and rounding up to 19 000; the other common wrong answer is 18 500, which is 18 475 to the nearest hundred rather than the nearest thousand.

html: Write 0.3 as a percentage.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 30 — that is 30%, and the scheme prints the bare number, B1 cao. A percentage is a number out of 100, so take the decimal to hundredths and read the top: 0.3 = 3⁄10 = 30⁄100 = 30%, which is the same move as × 100. The wrong answer to watch for is 3% — it comes from reading 0.3 as “three” rather than as three tenths. 0.03 is the one that is 3%.

lead: A diagram showing an angle marked y.
html: Write down the mathematical name for the type of angle marked y.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: reflex — B1 cao, and the scheme wants the word rather than a size. A reflex angle is anything bigger than 180° and smaller than 360°, so the arc marked y goes the long way round the point rather than the short way. Worth having ready as a set: acute under 90°, right angle exactly 90°, obtuse between 90° and 180°, straight line 180°, reflex over 180°. “Obtuse” is the answer to head off — it is what comes out when a student names the small angle at the point instead of the one the label is actually attached to.

html:
Write these numbers in order of size. Start with the smallest number.

0.21   0.2   0.03   0.1   0.16
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 0.03, 0.1, 0.16, 0.2, 0.21 — B1 for the complete list, and the scheme also accepts the reverse order, 0.21, 0.2, 0.16, 0.1, 0.03, even though the question asks for the smallest first. Pad every number to the same number of decimal places before comparing — 0.21, 0.20, 0.03, 0.10, 0.16 — and then they sort on the digits after the point as if those were whole numbers: 03, 10, 16, 20, 21. The trap is doing that comparison without padding, which makes 0.16 look bigger than 0.2 because 16 > 2. The mark is all-or-nothing, so writing the list out fresh is safer than numbering the printed ones.

html: Find the square root of 64
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 8 — B1, and the scheme says accept 8 or −8, so a student who has met the negative root is not penalised for giving it. The square root of 64 is the number that multiplies by itself to make 64: 8 × 8 = 64, and (−8) × (−8) = 64 as well, which is exactly why both are allowed. The wrong answer to watch for is 32 — halving instead of finding the number that squares to it.

html:
Ryan buys 4 cakes at £1.30 each and 2 identical tins of soup.

Ryan pays with a £10 note. He gets £1.80 change.

How much does Ryan pay for each tin of soup?
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: £1.5(0) — the bracket is the scheme’s: 1.50 and 1.5 both count, and it condones the answer written £1.5(0)p. Four marks, and three of them are for the route, so the working has to be on the page. P1 for either starting step — 4 × £1.30 = £5.2(0), or £10 − £1.80 = £8.2(0). P1 for putting the two together: £10 − £1.80 − “£5.20” = £3, or equivalent — the quotation marks are the scheme saying it follows through on whatever the student got for the four cakes. P1 for “£3” ÷ 2. A1 for 1.5(0) cao. Working entirely in pence is accepted throughout. The hard step is the second one: the £1.80 change has to come off as well as the cakes. A student who does £10 − £5.20 = £4.80 and halves it reaches £2.4(0), which reads like a finished answer — the scheme gives that a special case 2 marks and no more.

lead: Table of hours worked. Lena: Wed 6, Thu 9, Fri 8, Sat 6. Pavel: Wed 7, Thu 6, Fri 5, Sat 6.
html:
The table shows the number of hours that Lena and Pavel worked on each of four days last week.

On the grid, draw a suitable diagram or chart for this information.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: A fully labelled dual bar chart — and the scheme accepts a vertical line graph, a multiple or composite bar chart, or a frequency polygon for all four marks, so the kind of chart is not what is being tested. M1 for a key, or labels, that tell Lena and Pavel apart — unambiguous abbreviations such as L and P are accepted. M1 for 3 or 4 of the days labelled, or a linear scale present — the scale need not start at 0 for this mark, but it must be marked on the grid lines rather than in the spaces. M1 for bars, lines or points correctly showing the data for at least one person or two days, unambiguously right for whatever scale is drawn; for this mark the scheme also allows the four daily totals — 13, 15, 13, 12 — charted instead of the two people separately. C1 for a fully correct chart: days of the week labelled, vertical axis correctly scaled and labelled, and a key or labels for Lena and Pavel. For that last mark the scale must start at 0 and be linear across the range plotted. Condoned: “frequency” in place of “number of hours”, bars of unequal width, and no gaps or inconsistent gaps between them; the horizontal axis does not need an overall “day” label. The step that costs the fourth mark is the scale — deciding what one square is worth, and starting it at 0, before any bar is drawn.

lead: OA, OB and OC are three straight lines meeting at O. Angles 220 and 90 are marked, with x marked at C.
html: Work out the size of the angle marked x.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Angles at a Point & on a Line
answer: 50° — M1 for 360 − 220 − 90 or equivalent, A1 for 50 cao. The three lines all meet at O, so the angles round that point fill one complete turn and add to 360°: 220 + 90 = 310, and 360 − 310 = 50. The hard step is seeing that this is a point and not a straight line — reaching for 180 is the usual wrong turn. There is a second route the scheme explicitly allows for, extending one of AO, OC or BO and working with angles on a straight line; it is worth knowing about here because it changes which reason earns the mark in part (ii).

html: Give a reason for your answer.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Angles at a Point & on a Line
answer: Angles at a point add up to 360° — C1, and the scheme underlines angles at a point and 360, so both halves have to appear: the rule and the number. It also accepts “a full turn adds up to 360” and “full rotation is 360”. The list of what is not accepted is the more useful half, because every entry on it looks close enough to pass: “angles in a circle add to 360”, “a whole circle adds up to 360”, “it must add up to 360 degrees”, the arithmetic on its own (220 + 90 = 310, 360 − 310), “angles at a point add up to 180”, and “angles on a straight line add to 180”. One exception: if part (i) was worked by extending AO, OC or BO, then “angles on a straight line add to 180” does earn the mark, because it is the reason for that method. This is where reason marks go — a student with the right number who writes the sum out again instead of naming the rule scores nothing.

lead: A number machine: input, then x 2, then - 10, then output.
html: Work out the output when the input is 13
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 16 — run 13 through the boxes in the printed order: 13 × 2 = 26, then 26 − 10 = 16. B1, cao, and there is no method mark here, so the number is the whole of it. Two slips collect wrong answers: doing the boxes in the other order (13 − 10 = 3, then 3 × 2 = 6), and running the machine backwards.

html: Work out the input when the output is 28
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 19 — go back through the machine undoing each box: 28 + 10 = 38, then 38 ÷ 2 = 19. M1 for starting that inverse — the scheme wants 28 + 10 (= 38), or simply the sight of +10 and ÷2, and it says those two may be shown in a reversed flow diagram, or written next to the number machine printed in the question; A1 for 19, cao. Check forwards: 19 × 2 = 38, 38 − 10 = 28. The hard step is the order of the inverses — the LAST box is undone FIRST, so it is +10 then ÷2. Doing it the other way round (28 ÷ 2 = 14, 14 + 10 = 24) is the common wrong answer.

html: Show that there is a number for which the output is the same as the input.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: An input of 10 gives an output of 10 — 10 × 2 = 20, and 20 − 10 = 10, so output equals input. M1 for carrying out at least one trial (any value at all, as long as it is evaluated correctly), or for forming a suitable equation such as 2x − 10 = x, or just for identifying 10; C1 for actually showing that 10 goes in and 10 comes out. The scheme allows the single line 10 × 2 = 20 − 10 = 10 for M1 and C1 together, and it accepts a correct inverse-function trial too. If the trial is written on the number machine printed in the question it must be a value other than the 13 of part (a) or the 28 of part (b). Algebraically, 2x − 10 = x gives x = 10. The hard step is that this is a “show that”: writing 10 on its own earns the M1 and not the C1 — the arithmetic has to be on the page.

html:
There are 24 cows and 36 sheep on a farm.

Write as a ratio the number of cows to the number of sheep. Give your ratio in its simplest form.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2 : 3 — divide both numbers by 12, the highest common factor of 24 and 36: 24 ÷ 12 = 2 and 36 ÷ 12 = 3. M1 for any start — writing 24 : 36, or the reversed 3 : 2, or 1.5 : 1; A1 for 2 : 3, and the scheme also accepts 1 : 1.5, which is worth knowing because it is not whole numbers and still scores. Order is what gets lost: cows are named first, so it is 2 : 3 and not 3 : 2. And the scheme says do not ISW from 2 : 3 — subsequent working is not ignored here, so once 2 : 3 is written, carrying on and turning it into something else can throw the mark away. Stop at the simplified ratio.

html: Work out −12 ÷ −4
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 3 — a negative divided by a negative is positive, and 12 ÷ 4 = 3. B1, cao. The only thing being tested is the sign rule, and the answer it collects when that is missed is −3.

html: Find the value of [INDEX NOT EXTRACTED — printed as a power, shown in the paper as 2 to the 5th or 5 squared]
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 32 — 25 means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, which doubles up 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. B1, cao. The scheme settles which power the paper printed: 52 would be 25, and the answer given is 32, so the question is 2 to the fifth. The slip is multiplying the two numbers instead of repeating the multiplication — 2 × 5 = 10.
examiner_note: the mark scheme settles what this row lost in transcription: Find the value of 2 to the power 5 — i.e. Find the value of 25. The mark scheme's answer of 32 settles it: 52 would be 25, so the index printed in the paper is 25.

html:
Write one pair of brackets in this calculation so that the answer is correct.

30 ÷ 3 + 2 − 4 = 2
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 30 ÷ (3 + 2) − 4 — the brackets go round 3 + 2, so the division is by 5 instead of by 3: 30 ÷ 5 = 6, and 6 − 4 = 2. B1 for brackets correctly placed. Left alone, the order of operations does the division first and gives 10 + 2 − 4 = 8, so the whole job of the brackets is to push the addition in front of the division. One pair only, and it has to sit exactly there — 30 ÷ (3 + 2 − 4) is 30 ÷ 1 = 30, and (30 ÷ 3) + 2 − 4 is 8.

lead: Diagram of a triangle with sides 30 cm, 36 cm, 14 cm, and a rectangle of width 4 cm with the length unknown.
html:
The perimeter of the rectangle is a quarter of the perimeter of the triangle.

Work out the length of the rectangle.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 6 cm — three process marks and an accuracy mark, and the scheme walks it in this order. P1 for the perimeter of the triangle, 14 + 30 + 36 (= 80). P1 for a quarter of that, 80 ÷ 4 (= 20) — and the scheme explicitly gives BOTH of those marks for quartering each side instead and adding, 36 ÷ 4 + 14 ÷ 4 + 30 ÷ 4 (= 20). P1 for a complete process back to the length, (20 − 4 − 4) ÷ 2 or 20 ÷ 2 − 4. A1 for 6, cao. The hard step is the last one: a rectangle perimeter of 20 contains the 4 cm width twice, so 8 comes off and the remaining 12 is halved. Halving first gets there too — 20 ÷ 2 = 10 is one length plus one width, so 10 − 4 = 6. Subtracting a single 4 and halving gives 8, which is the wrong answer this question is built to collect.

lead: There are only £10 notes and £20 notes in a wallet. Ali takes at random a note from the wallet.
html: Write down the probability that Ali takes a note with a value of more than £5
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 1 — there are only £10 notes and £20 notes in the wallet and both are worth more than £5, so the event is certain and a certainty has probability 1. B1. The scheme also allows 100%, and any fraction of the form k⁄k such as 2⁄2. It does not accept a bare 100 (without the per-cent sign), and it does not accept the word certain — the question asks for a probability, which has to be written as a number on the 0-to-1 scale or as a percentage.

html:
There are only 1p coins and 2p coins in a bag. The total value of the coins in the bag is 40p. The total value of the 1p coins is the same as the total value of the 2p coins.

Simon takes at random a coin from the bag.

Find the probability that Simon takes a 1p coin.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2⁄3 — the 1p coins and the 2p coins are worth 20p each, so there are 20 one-penny coins and only 10 two-penny coins: 30 coins in the bag, 20 of which are 1p, and 20⁄30 = 2⁄3. P1 for any start on the proportions, and the scheme lists four routes that all earn it: writing a correct ratio such as 1p : 2p = 2 : 1; working out the counts, 40 ÷ 2 (= 20) and (40 ÷ 2) ÷ 2 (= 10); assigning any numbers in the right proportion, such as 6 one-penny coins and 3 two-penny coins; or finding the probability of a 2p instead, 1⁄3. A1 for 2⁄3 oe — any equivalent fraction, or decimal form 0.66(6…) or 0.67, or percentage form 66(.6…)% or 67%. The hard step is that equal VALUE is not equal NUMBER: 20p made of 1p coins is twice as many coins as 20p made of 2p coins, which is why the answer is 2⁄3 and not 1⁄2.

html: Work out 273 × 54
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 14742 — M1 for a complete correct method with the place value right: both lines of the long method (13650 and 1092), or the internal numbers of a grid, or a complete partitioning structure; M1, dependent on the first, for adding all the appropriate parts together; A1 for 14742, cao. By the grid the six parts are 200 × 50 = 10000, 70 × 50 = 3500, 3 × 50 = 150, 200 × 4 = 800, 70 × 4 = 280 and 3 × 4 = 12, and 10000 + 3500 + 150 + 800 + 280 + 12 = 14742. Place value is the whole of the first mark: the second line of the long method is 273 × 50 = 13650, not 1365, and in the grid the top-left cell is 10000 rather than 1000. And because the second M1 is dependent, adding up correctly on top of misplaced parts scores nothing at all.

Find the median.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 64 minutes — there are 15 times, so the median is the 8th, at position (15 + 1) ÷ 2 = 8, and a stem and leaf diagram already has them in order. Count the leaves along: 45, 49 (2 so far), 53, 57, 58 (5), 61, 62, 64 — the 8th is the third leaf on the 6 row, which the key reads as 64 minutes. B1, cao. Two slips: pointing at the middle of the DIAGRAM rather than the middle of the list (the 6 row is the longest, so it draws the eye), and giving the leaf 4 instead of the value 64.

html: Find the range.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 36 minutes — largest minus smallest, 81 − 45. M1 for identifying 81 and 45 as the two numbers that matter, shown as 81 − 45, or 45 − 81, or 45 to 81; A1 for 36, cao. The scheme is strict on two points. Marking them on the diagram is insufficient for the M1 — circling the leaves, or writing 1 and 5, does not count; the full values have to be written out. And an answer of −36 scores M1 A0: the range is a size, so it is never negative, however the subtraction was set down.

html:
Tessa also recorded the times that 15 children took to complete the run. For the children, the median was 75 minutes.

Compare the times that the adults took with the times that the children took.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: The adults were faster — their median of 64 minutes is lower than the children's 75, 11 minutes lower. C1 for one correct comparison of the medians, and it follows through from part (a), so it is marked against whatever median was found there. Statements the scheme names as acceptable: the adults were faster because they have the smaller median; the adults were 11 minutes faster on average; the adults were faster; the adults took less time; the children were slower; the children took more time; children took 11 minutes more on average; children had a larger median than the adults. Statements it refuses: the children were faster; the adults' median was 64, the children's median was 75; 11 minutes difference; the children had more time to run than the adults. The hard step is the one those refusals share — quoting the two medians side by side, or the gap between them, is not yet a comparison, because neither sentence says which group was quicker. Figures are not required, but if they appear they must be correct for the median found in (a), and the statement must be entirely true and not self-contradictory.

lead: Packs of batteries: pack of 4 costs £1.80, pack of 8 costs £3.20, pack of 12 costs £6.00.
html:
Batteries are sold in packs of 4, in packs of 8 and in packs of 12.

Which pack gives the best value for money? You must show how you get your answer.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
The pack of 8 — at 40p a battery against 45p for the pack of 4 and 50p for the pack of 12. "Supported" in the scheme's answer column is not decoration: correct answer with no supportive working scores 0 marks, so naming the right pack on its own earns nothing at all of the three.

P1 for a process of price ÷ quantity on at least two packs — at least two of 180 ÷ 4 (= 45), 320 ÷ 8 (= 40), 600 ÷ 12 (= 50). Pounds or pence both count. Any other route that lets two packs be compared also takes it, e.g. 180 × 2 (= 360) set against 320, or 320 ÷ 8 (= 40) then "40" × 12 (= 480) set against 600.

P1 for a complete process giving values that compare all three — the three unit prices together, or 3.20 ÷ 8 (= 0.40) then "0.40" × 4 (= 1.60) and "0.40" × 12 (= 4.80), or scaling everything to 24 batteries: 1.80 × 6 (= 10.80), 3.20 × 3 (= 9.60), 6.00 × 2 (= 12.00).

A1 for "pack of 8" with correct values covering all three packs.

The step that is actually hard is the one students think they have finished: comparing two pairs is not always enough. The scheme spells out which pairings settle it — 4 vs 8 together with 8 vs 12 works, and 4 vs 8 together with 4 vs 12 works, but 4 vs 12 together with 8 vs 12 does not, because the 4 and the 8 have then never been put side by side. Units matter too: the A mark is refused where inconsistent units would prevent the comparison, so "0.40p" written beside "45p" loses it even though the numbers are right.

html: Solve 2(4x − 5) = 18
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
x = 3.5 — and 31⁄2 or 7⁄2 are accepted equally (oe).

M1 for the first step, either way round: expand the bracket to 8x − 10 (= 18), or divide throughout by 2 first to get 4x − 5 = 9.

M1 for isolating the x term — 8x = 18 + 10, or 4x = 9 + 5 — and this mark follows through from their own equation of the form ax ± b = c, so a slip in the first step does not cost the second mark as well.

A1 for 3.5.

The thing to say out loud to a student: the scheme insists the step is carried out, not just intended. Writing "÷ 2" down both sides of 2(4x − 5) = 18 in the margin scores nothing on its own — the line 4x − 5 = k has to actually appear, with k anything other than 18 or 36 (18 is the right-hand side left untouched, 36 is it doubled instead of halved). Same for the second mark: 8x = k must be written, with k not 8 and not 18. The commonest wrong answer is 4.5, from expanding to 8x − 10 and then adding 10 to only one side.

html: Write down the value of [INDEX NOT EXTRACTED — printed as a power, shown in the paper as 10 to the power 0]
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
1 — B1, cao, the whole mark in one line with no method to show.

100 = 1, and so is any non-zero number raised to the power 0. The reason, if a student wants one: am ÷ an = am−n, so 103 ÷ 103 is both 100 and, obviously, 1. Or read the powers of ten downwards — 1000, 100, 10 — each one a tenth of the one before, so the next is 1.

cao means nothing else scores. The two answers students give here are 0 (reading the index as "ten lots of nothing") and 10 (reading the power 0 as leaving the number alone), and neither earns anything.

Note on this row: the library text lost the index — the question is printed as a power and the row records only that it was 10 to the power 0. The mark scheme's answer of 1 is consistent with that, though on its own it cannot confirm the base, since every non-zero base to the power 0 gives 1.
examiner_note: the mark scheme settles what this row lost in transcription: Write down the value of 10⁰ (10 to the power 0).

lead: Coordinate grid, x and y from -5 to 5, with triangles A and B drawn on it.
html: Describe fully the single transformation that maps triangle A onto triangle B.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Translation by the column vector ( 5−4) — 5 to the right and 4 down, written stacked in one pair of brackets. Two independent B1s: one for the word translation, one for the vector, so a student who names the transformation and gets the vector wrong still has a mark. The scheme will not take the vector in words — it says outright “do not accept 5 across, 4 down or 5 right, 4 down” — and will not take it written as a coordinate, (5, −4). It does condone the brackets being left off altogether, so a bare stacked 5 over −4 is fine. The trap is the last line of the scheme: no marks at all if more than one transformation is given, so “translation and reflection” scores zero even with the right vector — “describe fully the single transformation” means name one thing. Sitting beside a student, the step to slow down on is the sign: read across first, then up or down, and down is negative.

html:
Here are the first four terms of an arithmetic sequence.

1   5   9   13

Find an expression, in terms of n, for the nth term of this sequence.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: nth Term of a Linear Sequence
answer: 4n − 3 — B2, oe. The terms go up by 4 each time, so the nth term starts 4n; then 4 × 1 = 4 against a first term of 1, so subtract 3. Any equivalent form counts and any letter counts — 4x − 3 is accepted, and so are un = 4n − 3 and T = 4n − 3. B1 only for 4n + k where k is wrong or absent, provided it is unambiguously shown, so a bare 4n still banks one mark. B1 only, too, for n = 4n − 3 or “4nth − 3” — the right expression spoiled by writing it as something it is not, which is worth pointing out because it looks like a full answer. The step that actually goes wrong is jumping from the common difference straight to 4n + 1 off the first term; test the expression at n = 1 every time.

html: Work out 34⁄5 − 12⁄3
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 22⁄15, or 32⁄15 — oe, both count. M1 for a subtraction over a common denominator with at least one fraction converted correctly, then A1 for the value. Either route earns the M1 on its own: improper first, 34⁄5 − 12⁄3 = 19⁄5 − 5⁄3 = 57⁄15 − 25⁄15; or keep the whole numbers, (3)12⁄15 − (1)10⁄15. Two tolerances worth knowing, because they change what a student should do after they have the answer: 32⁄15 left improper is full marks, and the scheme says ISW — a wrong conversion to a mixed number after a correct 32⁄15, or a botched simplification of it, is ignored rather than penalised. Against that, decimals get no credit at all unless they lead to a correct fraction. The step to name is the common denominator itself: fifteenths for both, and only one of the two needs to be right to bank the method mark.

lead: Kevin was asked to work out 2 1/3 x 5/8. His working: 7/3 x 5/8 = 35/24 = 1 9/24
html:
Kevin’s answer is wrong.

What mistake has Kevin made?
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Kevin did not convert 35⁄24 into the correct mixed number — 35⁄24 is 111⁄24, not 19⁄24 — C1 for explaining that, and only that; the multiplication itself, 7⁄3 × 5⁄8 = 35⁄24, is right. The scheme accepts “the 9 should be 11”, “in his answer 9⁄24 should have been 11⁄24”, “he has not got the numerator right in his final answer”, “he simplified into the mixed number incorrectly”, “he has not put the remainder as the numerator”, and either arithmetic version — 19⁄24 would give 33⁄24, or 35⁄24 = 111⁄24. It explicitly refuses the vague ones, and that is the whole difficulty of this mark: “he converted the fraction wrongly” scores nothing, and neither do “he should have used a common denominator”, “he has not simplified his answer”, “he should have done keep, flip, change” or “the answer should be 110⁄24”. Naming the number — 11, not 9 — is what earns it. Figures written in the question space count towards the explanation.

lead: The diagram shows a plan of a floor. Dimensions 10 m, 6 m, 8 m, 5 m.
html:
Petra is going to cover the floor with paint.

Petra has 3 tins of paint. There are 2.5 litres of paint in each tin. Petra thinks 1 litre of paint will cover 10 m2 of floor.

Assuming Petra is correct, does she have enough paint to cover the floor?
You must show all your working.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Yes — the floor is 68 m2 and 3 tins cover 75 m2, so she has enough. Four marks and three of them are the route. P1 for the area of any one piece: 10 × 8 (= 80), 10 × 5 (= 50), 8 × 6 (= 48), (10 − 6) × 5 (= 20), (10 − 6) × (8 − 5) (= 12), 6 × (8 − 5) (= 18) or 5 × 6 (= 30) — but the scheme withholds it if they go on to multiply by a third length, which is the commonest way this mark is lost. P1 for a complete area: cut it off a rectangle, “80” − “12”, or split it, “50” + “18” or “48” + “20” — all three give 68. P1 for comparing on any one of three scales: 3 × 2.5 × 10 (= 75 m2 covered), or “68” ÷ 10 (= 6.8 litres needed), or “68” ÷ 10 ÷ 2.5 (= 2.72 tins needed) — and it follows through on whatever area they believe they have. A1 for Yes supported by a matching pair of figures: 68 and 75, or 6.8 and 7.5, or 68 and 2.72. The decision on its own is not the mark; the numbers have to be on the page beside it. A wrong statement about how much paint is left over is ignored provided the correct figures are there. The hard step is the side nobody gives you: the plan prints 10, 6, 8 and 5, and the missing piece is (10 − 6) by (8 − 5).

lead: Actually, 1 litre of paint will cover 11 m2 of floor.
html:
Does this affect your answer to part (a)?
You must give a reason for your answer.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: No effect — she still has enough. One mark, C1, and it follows through from part (a), so there has to be a decision in (a) for it to follow through from. The mark is for a decision plus a reason together. The scheme’s acceptable answers are “no effect, she will need less paint”, “it won’t change, she will still have enough”, “no, she will have more paint left over”, and “no, as this will cover 82.5 m<sup>2</sup>” (7.5 litres × 11). It also prints the near misses, and they are the thing to point out: “Petra will need less paint” and “she will have more paint left over” are refused — both are true, and both leave the decision off. “She won’t have enough paint” and “she will need more paint” are refused as wrong. Any figures written into the statement must be correct for the area claimed in (a). So the sentence needs the word yes, no or “no effect” in it, and covering more per litre can only help.

name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
html: Venn diagram, sets P and Q inside universal set E. P only: 12, 18. Intersection: 15. Q only: 10, 14. Outside both circles: 11, 13, 16, 17.
Write down the numbers that are in set P′
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 17 — B1, cao, so it is the whole list or nothing. P′ is everything in the universal set that is NOT inside circle P: the two numbers in Q alone (10 and 14) plus the four outside both circles (11, 13, 16, 17). P itself is 12, 15 and 18, and 15 is the one students lose — it sits in the overlap, so it is in P and must be left out of P′.

html:
A number is chosen at random from the universal set, E

Find the probability that this number is in the set P ∪ Q
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Venn Diagrams & Set Notation, Basic Probability
answer: 5⁄9 — five of the nine numbers in the universal set lie inside one circle or the other. M1 for identifying that set: 10, 12, 14, 15, 18. P ∪ Q is everything in either circle, and the number they share is counted once, not twice. The scheme also gives the M1 for work that shows the right half of the fraction without the other: a⁄9 with a a whole number from 1 to 8, or 5⁄b with b a whole number above 5, or the right numbers in the wrong form, eg 5 : 9. A1 is “oe” and generous with it: any equivalent fraction, or the decimal 0.55(5…) or 0.56, or the percentage 55(.5…)% or 56%. Two things cost the marks — reading ∪ (union, either circle) as ∩ (intersection, the overlap only), and double-counting the overlap to get 6⁄9. Reading the diagram: the overlap holds 15, so P ∪ Q is 12 and 18 from P, 10 and 14 from Q, and 15 from the middle.

html:
Sophie drives a distance of 513 kilometres on a motorway in France.

She pays 0.81 euros for every 10 kilometres she drives.

Work out an estimate for the total amount that Sophie pays.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 40 euros — 500 ÷ 10 × 0.8, rounding both numbers to 1 significant figure first. The answer column says “estimated value” rather than a number on purpose: the A1 follows through whatever rounding the student chose, so 40.8 (from 510) and 40.5 (from 500 × 0.81) are each worth full marks. P1 for a 1sf value actually used in a calculation — 500 ÷ 10, or 500 × 0.8, or 510 × 0.8, or 513 × 0.8, or 500 × 0.81. The rounding may come after a correct step: 513 ÷ 10 = 51.3 → 50, then 50 × 0.81 scores both process marks, as does 51 × 0.8. P1 for a full process to the total — 500 ÷ 10 × 0.8 (= 40), or 510 ÷ 10 × 0.8 (= 40.8), or 500 ÷ 10 × 0.81 (= 40.5), or in general [distance] ÷ 10 × [amount]; the unrounded 513 ÷ 10 × 0.81 is accepted for this mark too. A1 for the answer their own rounded values give. Two tolerances the scheme states outright: 0.81 rounded to 0.80 is accepted, and 0.81 rounded to 1 is condoned for the process marks but loses the A1. The step that is actually hard is the ÷ 10 — 0.81 euros buys 10 kilometres, not one, so 500 × 0.8 = 400 euros is the answer to watch for.

html:
Is your answer to part (a) an underestimate or an overestimate?
Give a reason for your answer.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: An underestimate — because both numbers were rounded down: 513 km down to 500 km and 0.81 euros down to 0.80, so the estimate is less than the true cost. C1, following through from part (a). The scheme puts two conditions on it. The reason must be about the estimating — the rounding done at the start — and not about rounding the final answer at the end. And there must be a final answer in (a) for this to follow through from, so a student who abandoned (a) cannot pick the mark up here. A bare “underestimate” with no reason does not score; the word “down” is doing the work.

lead: Straight line L drawn on a coordinate grid, x from -4 to 4, y from -3 to 7.
html: Find an equation for L.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Equation of a Line, Straight Line Graphs
answer: y = 3⁄2x + 3 — or y = 1.5x + 3, and “oe”, so 2y = 3x + 6 is equally full marks. The line crosses the y-axis at 3 and climbs 3 for every 2 across. M1 for a correct method for the gradient: (6 − 3) ÷ (2 − 0) = 3⁄2 off two points on the line, or identifying 3 as the intercept in words or in a partial equation, or writing y = 3⁄2x + c, or y − b = 3⁄2(x − a) for a correct point (a, b). The scheme is specific that just circling the 3 on the grid is not enough, and that the c has to appear as a letter or a number. M1 for assembling it — y = 3⁄2x (+ c), or their own gradient with the 3 in place, or y − y1 = 3⁄2(x − x1); earning this one implies the first. A1 for any correct equation, in any form. The mark that goes missing is the gradient: it is rise over run, so 2⁄3 is the classic inversion, and a grid whose squares are not one unit each will punish counting squares without checking the scale.

lead: M is a different straight line with equation y = 5x
html: Write down the equation of a straight line parallel to M.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Any equation of the form y = 5x + c with c ≠ 0 — eg y = 5x + 1. B1. The answer column just says “equation” because there is no single right one. Parallel means the same gradient, so the 5 must survive untouched; the only thing that may change is the intercept. c ≠ 0 is the condition students fall over: y = 5x is M itself, and the question asks for a line parallel to M, which means a different line. Any equivalent form is accepted, so 5x − y + 1 = 0 or y − 1 = 5x also score.

html:
Kasim has some small jars, some medium jars and some large jars. He has a total of 400 jars.

3⁄8 of the 400 jars are empty.

For the empty jars,
number of small jars : number of medium jars = 3 : 4
number of medium jars : number of large jars = 1 : 2

Work out the percentage of Kasim’s jars that are empty small jars.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Fractions of an Amount, Sharing in a Ratio, Percentage of an Amount
answer: 7.5 — that is 7.5%, and the scheme takes 7<sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>2</sub> or any equivalent. Five marks, four of them process. P1 for the number of empty jars: <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> × 400 = 150. P1 for the start of the ratio work, and this is the step the question is really testing — 3 : 4 and 1 : 2 do not join up until the mediums agree, so scale the second to 4 : 8 and chain them into small : medium : large = 3 : 4 : 8. P1 for the empty small jars: <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>3 + 4 + 8</sub> × “150” = 30, or writing the whole split out as 30 : 40 : 80. P1 for turning that into a percentage: 30 ÷ 400 × 100. A1 for 7.5. The scheme prints a second route worth the same five marks and it is shorter if a student can see it: chain to 3 : 4 : 8, so small jars are <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>15</sub> = <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> of the empty ones, then <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> × <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> = <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>40</sub> of all the jars, and <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>40</sub> × 100 = 7.5 — the 400 is never needed at all. Two wrong answers to watch for: 30, which is the count of jars offered as if it were the percentage, and 20%, from dividing 30 by the 150 empty jars instead of by all 400.

html:
In a sale, normal prices are reduced by 30%

The sale price of a TV is £280

Work out the normal price of the TV.
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 400 — M1 for 280 ÷ 0.7 oe, A1 cao. A 30% reduction leaves 70%, so the £280 sale price IS 70% of the normal price — and you get back to the whole by dividing, not by adding 30% on. 280 ÷ 0.7 = 400. Check it forwards: 30% of 400 is 120, and 400 − 120 = 280. The wrong answer to head off is 364: that is 280 + 30% of 280, which takes the percentage of the wrong number — the reduction was 30% of 400, not of 280.

html: Solve x + 11 [INEQUALITY SIGN NOT EXTRACTED] 5 − 1⁄2x
name: Paper 1 (Non-calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: x ≤ −4 — M1 for a correct first step, M1 for a full method or for the critical value −4, A1 for x ≤ −4 oe. Clear the half first by doubling everything: 2x + 22 ≤ 10 − x. Then add x to both sides, 3x + 22 ≤ 10, and take 22 off: 3x ≤ −12, so x ≤ −4. The scheme gives 2 of the 3 marks for −4 written with an = or the wrong inequality sign, so the final mark is the sign itself — and because nothing here was multiplied or divided by a negative, the sign never flips.

answer: 0.31 — B1 cao, and .31 is accepted. Hundredths are the second decimal place, so 31 hundredths is 0.31 — no dividing needed once you read it that way.

html: Write down the multiple of 7 that is between 30 and 40
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 35 — B1 cao. The sevens either side are 28 and 42, so 35 is the only one in between. 5 × 7 = 35.

html:
Complete the statement below to make it correct.

     × m = 2m
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2 — B1 cao. Whatever goes in the box is multiplied by m to give 2m, and 2 × m is 2m.

lead: A pictogram of houses sold in January to May. Key: one symbol represents 4 houses. January, February and March are filled in.
html:
Ben sells houses. The pictogram shows information about the number of houses Ben sold in each of the first three months of last year.

Write down the number of houses Ben sold in January.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 10 — B1 cao. One symbol is 4 houses, and January shows two whole symbols and a half, so 4 + 4 + 2 = 10.

lead: In April, Ben sold 11 houses.
html: Show this information on the pictogram.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2 full squares and 3 quarters of a square — B1. 11 houses at 4 to a symbol is 11 ÷ 4 = 2¾ symbols. The scheme allows the three quarters drawn as eleven separate quarter-squares, or as a half plus a quarter.

html:
Ben sold a total of 60 houses in the first five months of last year.

Work out the number of houses Ben sold in May.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 18 — P1 P1 A1. Read the first three months off the pictogram: January 10 (from part (a)), February 4 + 4 + 1 = 9, March 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. April is the 11 you drew. That is 10 + 9 + 12 + 11 = 42, so May is 60 − 42 = 18. The scheme wants 18 written down for full marks — drawing the squares for May alone earns P2, not A1.

lead: A printed line to be measured.
html: Measure the length of this line. Give your answer in centimetres.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 8.7 cm — B1, and anything from 8.5 to 8.9 is accepted. Line the zero of the ruler up with the end of the line, not the ruler’s own edge, which is the usual half-centimetre lost.

lead: An angle marked x, to be measured with a protractor.
html: Measure the size of the angle marked x.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 67° — B1, and anything from 65 to 69 is accepted. Read the scale that starts at zero on one arm; the protractor carries two, and taking the wrong one gives 113, which is 180 − 67.

html: In the space below, draw a hexagon.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: A 6-sided shape — B1. Any hexagon counts and it does not have to be regular; the scheme allows free-hand drawing. Count the sides before you stop — five and seven are what get drawn under time pressure.

lead: Points A and B shown on a coordinate grid, x and y from -6 to 6.
html: Write down the coordinates of the point A.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: (2, 1) — B1 cao. Along the corridor then up the stairs: x first.

html: Find the coordinates of the midpoint of AB.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: (0, −2) — M1 A1. The midpoint is the mean of each coordinate: x = (2 + −2) ÷ 2 = 0 and y = (1 + −5) ÷ 2 = −2. Writing it as (−2, 0) — the right numbers the wrong way round — is specifically named in the scheme and scores 1 of the 2.

html: On the grid, mark with a cross the point with coordinates (−4, 2). Label this point C.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: C marked at (−4, 2) — C1 cao. Four to the LEFT and two up.

html:
Anil has a job as a driver. He is paid for each mile he drives. He is also paid expenses.

One week Anil writes down the distance readings from his car.
Start of week: 47241 miles
End of week: 47879 miles

For this week, Anil is paid 47p for each mile he drives. He is also paid expenses of £80

Work out the total amount that Anil is paid. Give your answer in pounds.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: £379.86 — P1 P1 B1 A1. The miles driven are the difference between the two readings: 47879 − 47241 = 638. At 47p each that is 638 × 47 = 29986p, which is £299.86, and the expenses go on top: 299.86 + 80 = 379.86. One of the four marks is for converting between pence and pounds at all, which is where this question is usually lost — an answer of 30066 is the same work with the units left in pence.

html:
Anita throws a coin 3 times. Each time the coin can land on heads (H) or tails (T).

List all the possible outcomes.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT — M1 A1, all eight with no repeats and nothing extra. Three coins with two faces each is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 outcomes, so if you have not got eight you have missed one. Listing them in a fixed order — all the H-firsts, then all the T-firsts — is what stops that. M1 alone for any three correct.

lead: A spinner divided into three unequal sections labelled 1, 2 and 3.
html:
Majid is going to spin the arrow. The arrow can land on 1 or on 2 or on 3.

Majid says, “The probability that the arrow will land on 2 is 1⁄3 because the spinner has three sections.”

Is Majid correct? You must give a reason for your answer.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: No, with a reason — C1. The three sections are not the same size, so they are not equally likely and you cannot just divide 1 by 3. Section 2 is the right angle, a quarter of the circle, so its probability is 1⁄4. The scheme accepts any of: the sections are different sizes; 1 and 3 are more likely than 2; 2 should be a quarter; 2 is less than a third. It specifically REFUSES “2 has a 90° angle” on its own — that is an observation, not a reason.

html:
Saira buys 24 bars of chocolate. 2⁄3 of the 24 bars are white chocolate. The rest of the 24 bars are milk chocolate.

Each milk chocolate bar has a weight of 35 grams.

Work out the total weight of the milk chocolate bars that Saira buys.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 280 g — P1 P1 A1. Two thirds of 24 are white, so 24 ÷ 3 × 2 = 16 white and the rest, 24 − 16 = 8, are milk. Each milk bar is 35 g, so 8 × 35 = 280. The trap is answering for the WHITE bars: 16 × 35 = 560, which the scheme names and gives 2 of the 3 marks for.

html: Simplify 2c × 3d
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 6cd — B1. Multiply the numbers and write the letters together: 2 × 3 = 6. 6dc is fine; leaving the times sign in, as 6 × cd, scores zero.

lead: T = x + 2y, with x = 3 and y = -4
html: Work out the value of T.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: −5 — M1 A1. T = x + 2y = 3 + 2 × −4 = 3 − 8 = −5. Multiply before you add — doing 3 + 2 first gives 5 × −4 = −20.

html:
On Monday, Lizzie cycled 36 kilometres in 3 hours.

Work out Lizzie’s average speed.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 12 km/h — M1 A1 cao. Speed is distance divided by time: 36 ÷ 3 = 12.

html:
On Tuesday, Lizzie cycled 36 kilometres at an average speed of 16 kilometres per hour.

Lizzie says that the total time she cycled on Monday and Tuesday was less than 5 hours 20 minutes.

Is Lizzie correct? You must show how you get your answer.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Yes, with figures — P1 P1 C1. Tuesday took 36 ÷ 16 = 2.25 hours, which is 2 hours 15 minutes. With Monday’s 3 hours that is 5.25 hours = 5 hours 15 minutes, and 5 h 15 min IS less than 5 h 20 min, so Lizzie is right. The mark is for the FIGURES, not the word — and 5.25 hours is 5 hours 15 minutes, not 5 hours 25, which is the decimal-time trap this question is built on.

html:
£3500 is invested in a bank for 6 years. The bank pays simple interest at a rate of 2.5% per year.

Work out the total amount of simple interest paid.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: £525 — M1 A1 cao. Simple interest is the same each year: 2.5% of 3500 is 3500 × 0.025 = £87.50, and 87.50 × 6 = 525. It asks for the INTEREST, not the total in the bank — £4025 is the balance and scores 1.

lead: A conversion graph between ounges and grams, grams from 0 to 300 and ounces from 0 to 10.
html:
You can use this graph to change between ounces and grams.

Change 6 ounces to grams.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 170 g — B1, anything from 167 to 173 accepted. Go up from 6 on the ounces axis to the line, then across to the grams axis.

html: Change 1 kg to ounces.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 35 ounces — M1 A1, anything from 34 to 36 accepted. The graph only goes to 300 g and 1 kg is 1000 g, so you have to scale: read a point you can see, say 200 g ≈ 7 ounces, then 1000 is 5 × 200 so multiply the ounces by 5. Reading 1 kg straight off a graph that stops at 300 g is the thing to notice.

lead: Triangle ABC drawn accurately.
html:
The region R consists of all points inside the triangle that are less than 4 cm from A and closer to C than to B.

On the diagram show, by shading, the region R.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Region R shaded — C1 C1 C1, one mark each for the arc, the bisector and the region. “Less than 4 cm from A” is an arc of radius 4 cm centred on A, and you want INSIDE it. “Closer to C than to B” is the perpendicular bisector of CB, and you want the C side. R is the overlap of those two, inside the triangle. Free-hand is allowed, and the region only needs to be unambiguous — shading is enough without the letter R.

html:
Mrs Simpson organised a school trip for 66 children. The total cost of the trip was £1800

The school paid 56% of the total cost. The rest of the total cost was divided equally between the 66 children.

Work out how much money each child paid.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: £12 — P1 P1 A1. The school paid 56%, so the parents paid the other 44%: 1800 × 0.44 = £792. Split between 66 children, 792 ÷ 66 = 12. Working out 56% and dividing that is the wrong half — the question asks what each CHILD paid.

html:
Work out the value of √(35.2 + 1.73)4.62 − 8.91

Write down all the numbers on your calculator display.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Order of Operations, Laws of Indices
answer: 0.5170189759 — M1 A1. Do the top and the bottom separately. Top: 1.73 = 4.913, so 35.2 + 4.913 = 40.113, and √40.113 = 6.333482454. Bottom: 4.62 = 21.16, so 21.16 − 8.91 = 12.25. Then 6.333482454 ÷ 12.25 = 0.5170189759. It says write down ALL the numbers on the display, so give at least three decimal places — the scheme checks the first three significant figures.

html: Write your answer to part (a) correct to 2 significant figures.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 0.52 — B1. Two significant figures counts from the first non-zero digit, so the 5 and the 1, and the 7 after them rounds the 1 up. The scheme refuses a trailing zero: 0.520 is three figures, not two.

lead: ABC is a right-angled triangle. AB = 19 cm, AC = 10 cm.
html: Work out the length of CB. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 16.2 cm — M1 A1, anything from 16.1 to 16.2 accepted. AB = 19 is the longest side, so it is the hypotenuse and this is Pythagoras backwards: CB2 = 192 − 102 = 361 − 100 = 261, and √261 = 16.155…, which is 16.2 to 3 significant figures. Adding instead of subtracting gives 21.5 and no marks.

html: Write 90 as a product of its prime factors.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 — M1 A1, and 2 × 32 × 5 is accepted. Split 90 until only primes are left: 90 = 9 × 10 = 3 × 3 × 2 × 5. Check by multiplying back.

html:
A = 22 × 3, B = 2 × 32

Write down the lowest common multiple (LCM) of A and B.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 36 — B1, and 22 × 32 is accepted. A = 22 × 3 = 12 and B = 2 × 32 = 18. For the LOWEST common multiple take the HIGHEST power of each prime that appears: 22 and 32, so 4 × 9 = 36. Taking the lowest powers gives 6, which is the HCF.

html:
The number of hours, H, that some machines take to make 5000 bottles is given by H = 72⁄n where n is the number of machines.

On Monday, 6 machines made 5000 bottles.
On Tuesday, 9 machines made 5000 bottles.

The machines took more time to make the bottles on Monday than on Tuesday.

How much more time?
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 4 hours — M1 A1 cao. Put each number of machines into H = 72 ÷ n: Monday 72 ÷ 6 = 12 hours, Tuesday 72 ÷ 9 = 8 hours. The question asks how much MORE time, so subtract: 12 − 8 = 4. More machines means fewer hours, which is why the answer is a difference and not a total.

html:
There are only red discs, blue discs and yellow discs in a bag. There are 24 yellow discs in the bag.

Mel is going to take at random a disc from the bag. The probability that the disc will be yellow is 0.16

the number of red discs : the number of blue discs = 5 : 4

Work out the number of red discs in the bag.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Basic Probability, Sharing in a Ratio
answer: 70 — P1 P1 P1 A1. The 24 yellow discs are 0.16 of the bag, so the bag holds 24 ÷ 0.16 = 150 discs. That leaves 150 − 24 = 126 red and blue together, shared 5 : 4 — nine parts, so 126 ÷ 9 = 14 per part and red is 5 × 14 = 70. Blue is 56, and the scheme insists that if you find both you must say which one is the answer.

lead: Table of values for y = x^2 - x. x values -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3. Given y values: 6 at x = -2, 0 at x = 0, 2 at x = 2.
html: Complete the table of values for y = x2 − x
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2, 0, 6 — B2 for all three, B1 for one or two. Square first, then subtract x: at x = −1, (−1)2 − (−1) = 1 + 1 = 2; at x = 1, 1 − 1 = 0; at x = 3, 9 − 3 = 6. Squaring a negative gives a positive and then subtracting a negative adds — that double sign is the whole of the first one.

html: On the grid, draw the graph of y = x2 − x for values of x from −2 to 3
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: A smooth curve through (−2, 6), (−1, 2), (0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 2), (3, 6) — B2, or B1 for plotting at least five of your own points correctly. It is a parabola with its lowest point half way between x = 0 and x = 1. A curve drawn free-hand is fine; joining the points with straight line segments is not.

html: Use your graph to find estimates for the solutions of the equation x2 − x = 4
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: −1.6 and 2.6 — M1 A1, anything in −1.7 to −1.5 and 2.5 to 2.7 accepted. Draw the line y = 4 across your curve and read off where they cross. The scheme gives zero for solving it algebraically — the question says use your graph, so the graph is the method being marked.

html:
Andy, Luke and Tina share some sweets in the ratio 1 : 6 : 14

Tina gives 3⁄7 of her sweets to Andy. Tina then gives 12½% of the rest of her sweets to Luke.

Tina says, “Now all three of us have the same number of sweets.”

Is Tina correct? You must show how you get your answer.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Sharing in a Ratio, Fractions of an Amount, Percentage of an Amount
answer: Yes — P1 P1 P1 C1, and the figures have to be shown. Work in parts: the ratio 1 : 6 : 14 is 21 parts, so Andy 1, Luke 6, Tina 14. Tina gives 3⁄7 of her 14 = 6 to Andy, so Andy has 1 + 6 = 7 and Tina has 14 − 6 = 8 left. She then gives 12½% — an eighth — of those 8 to Luke, which is 1, so Luke has 6 + 1 = 7 and Tina keeps 8 − 1 = 7. All three have 7 parts, so Tina is right. The scheme is explicit: accurate figures with no supporting working score 0.

lead: Quadrilateral ABCD with angles 2x + 15, 4x + 15, 4x + 8, 3x - 3 marked, all in degrees.
html: Show that ABCD is a trapezium.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Angles in Triangles & Quadrilaterals, Angles in Parallel Lines, Linear Equations
answer: Shown — M1 M1 A1 C1. The four angles of a quadrilateral add to 360, so (2x + 15) + (4x + 15) + (4x + 8) + (3x − 3) = 360, which is 13x + 35 = 360, so 13x = 325 and x = 25. The angles are then 65°, 115°, 108° and 72°. Now 65 + 115 = 180, and co-interior angles that add to 180 mean those two sides are parallel — so ABCD has a pair of parallel sides and is a trapezium. The other pair, 65 + 72 = 137, is NOT 180, which is what stops it being a parallelogram. The last mark is for SAYING that: “co-interior angles sum to 180, so the lines are parallel”.

lead: Two similar isosceles triangles ABC and DEF. ABC has base 6 cm and equal sides 8 cm. DEF has base 1.5 cm.
html:
DE = DF

Work out the length of DE.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2 cm — M1 A1 cao. The bases correspond: 6 cm goes to 1.5 cm, so the scale factor is 1.5 ÷ 6 = 1⁄4. The equal sides go the same way: 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Multiplying by 4 instead of dividing gives 32 — check which triangle is the smaller before you start.

html:
The table shows information about the weights of 120 oranges.

Find the class interval that contains the median.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 100 < w ≤ 150 — B1 cao. With 120 oranges the median sits between the 60th and 61st. Running totals are 34, then 34 + 29 = 63 — so the 60th and 61st are both inside the second class. The answer is the CLASS, not a number.

html: Calculate an estimate for the mean weight of the 120 oranges. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 152 g — M1 M1 A1, anything from 151 to 152 accepted. Use the midpoint of each class: 75, 125, 175, 225, 275. Multiply each by its frequency — 75×34 = 2550, 125×29 = 3625, 175×27 = 4725, 225×19 = 4275, 275×11 = 3025 — which total 18200. Then divide by the 120 oranges: 18200 ÷ 120 = 151.66…, so 152 to 3 significant figures. Dividing by 5 instead of 120 is named in the scheme as the method that scores nothing.

html: Write 23% as a fraction.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: <sup>23</sup>⁄<sub>100</sub> — B1, or any equivalent. Per cent means “out of a hundred”, so 23% is 23 out of 100. It does not have to be cancelled.

html: Change 800 centimetres to metres.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 8 metres — B1 cao. There are 100 centimetres in a metre, so divide by 100: 800 ÷ 100 = 8.

html: Write down the value of the 3 in the number 62837
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: tens, or 30 — B1. In 62837 the digits are ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, TENS, units, so the 3 sits in the tens column and is worth 30. Either answer is accepted, and the spelling is condoned if the meaning is clear.

html: Simplify 7a + a − 5a
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 3a — B1. They are all lots of a, so just count them: 7 + 1 − 5 = 3. The lone a counts as one, which is the one people drop.

html:
Write the following fractions in order of size. Start with the smallest fraction.

1⁄2   2⁄3   1⁄4
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>4</sub>, <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>2</sub>, <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> — B1. Put them over a common denominator of 12: 3⁄12, 6⁄12, 8⁄12. A bigger number on the bottom makes a SMALLER fraction when the tops match, which is why a quarter is the smallest here. Decimals or percentages are accepted as working.

lead: A map has a scale of 1 cm represents 4 km.
html:
On the map, the distance from town A to town B is 8 cm.

Work out the real distance, in km, from town A to town B.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 32 km — P1 A1 cao. Each centimetre on the map is 4 real kilometres, so 8 × 4 = 32.

html:
The real length of a road is 10 km.

Work out the length of the road on the map. Give the units of your answer.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2.5 cm — P1 A1, and the UNITS are part of the answer here. Going the other way you divide: 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5. The scheme accepts 25 mm or 0.025 m, but a bare 2.5 with no unit gets nothing — the question asks for the units outright.

lead: A bar chart of methods of travel to school: Bus, Car, Cycle, Walk, Other, with a vertical axis from 0 to 10 students.
html:
Julie asks some students how they travel to school. The chart shows her results.

Write down which method of travel is the mode.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Bus — B1 cao. The mode is the tallest bar, and the answer is the CATEGORY, not how many students it holds.

html: More students walk to school than cycle to school. How many more?
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 5 — B1 cao. Read both bars and subtract: walk minus cycle. “How many more” is a difference, not the bigger number.

html:
Aisha was born in 1993. There was an election in the year of Aisha’s 18th birthday. There is an election every 5 years.

Will there be an election in 2030? You must show how you get your answer.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: No, with figures — P1 P1 A1. Aisha turned 18 in 1993 + 18 = 2011, and that was an election year. Elections are every 5 years, so they fall in 2011, 2016, 2021, 2026, 2031 — 2030 is not one of them. The scheme also takes the shorter argument: election years from 2011 end in 1 or 6, and 2030 ends in 0.

html:
Lucia is going on a skiing holiday. The cost of ski hire is £26 per day. The cost of a lift pass is £45 per day. The cost of ski lessons is £23.50 per hour.

Lucia will pay for ski hire for 5 days, a lift pass for 4 days and ski lessons for 8 hours. Lucia has £500

Show that Lucia has enough money to pay for the total cost of ski hire, the lift pass and the ski lessons.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Shown — P1 P1 C1, and the working is the answer. Ski hire 5 × 26 = £130; lift pass 4 × 45 = £180; lessons 8 × 23.50 = £188. Total = 130 + 180 + 188 = £498, which is less than £500, so she has enough — with £2 to spare. Watch the three different units: days, days and HOURS.

lead: A circle drawn on the page.
html: On the diagram above, draw a radius of the circle.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: A radius drawn — B1: any straight line from the centre to the edge. Free-hand is fine. A line all the way across would be a diameter, which is not what was asked.

lead: Another circle with a straight line drawn inside it.
html: Write down the mathematical name for the straight line inside this circle.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Chord — B1 cao. A chord joins two points on the circle without going through the centre; through the centre it would be a diameter.

html:
There are 8 episodes in a TV series. Each episode lasts 45 minutes.

Work out the total time that the 8 episodes last. Give your answer in hours.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 6 hours — M1 A1 cao. 8 episodes × 45 minutes = 360 minutes, and 360 ÷ 60 = 6 hours. It asks for HOURS, so 360 on its own scores 1 of the 2.

html: Write down three prime numbers that are between 20 and 40
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Any three of 23, 29, 31, 37 — M1 A1. A prime has exactly two factors, so strike out everything even and everything ending in 5, then check 21 (3×7), 27 (3×9), 33 (3×11) and 39 (3×13). Four correct with none wrong is also accepted; one wrong number among three loses the A mark.

lead: Two-way table of favourite language by year group. Columns: French, German, Spanish, Total. Year 10: French 33, Spanish 34. Year 11: German 45, Total 113. Totals row: Spanish 67, overall 207. Every other cell is blank.
html:
James asks students in Year 10 and Year 11 to name their favourite language from French or German or Spanish. The two-way table shows information about his results.

Complete the two-way table.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Year 10: 33, 27, 34, 94. Year 11: 35, 45, 33, 113. Total: 68, 72, 67, 207. — B3 for all six, B2 for four or five, B1 for two or three. Work from the rows and columns that have only one gap. Spanish column: 67 − 34 = 33 for Year 11. Year 11 row: 113 − 45 − 33 = 35. Year 10 total: 207 − 113 = 94, so Year 10 German is 94 − 33 − 34 = 27. Then the column totals: French 33 + 35 = 68, German 27 + 45 = 72. Check at the end: 68 + 72 + 67 = 207.

lead: Table of drinks ordered in a cafe. Coffee 30, Hot chocolate 10, Tea 50.
html:
The table gives information about the drinks people ordered in a cafe.

Draw an accurate pie chart for this information.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Pie chart with coffee 120°, hot chocolate 40°, tea 200° — M1 A1 A1. There are 30 + 10 + 50 = 90 drinks in a whole circle of 360°, so each drink is 360 ÷ 90 = 4°. Then 30 × 4 = 120, 10 × 4 = 40, 50 × 4 = 200 — and they must total 360, which is the check. The scheme requires each sector to be labelled with the DRINK, not with the angle.

html:
Which is greater, 15% of 88 or 20% of 62?

You must show all your working.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 15% of 88 is greater — P1 P1 C1. Work both out: 15% of 88 = 0.15 × 88 = 13.2, and 20% of 62 = 0.2 × 62 = 12.4. 13.2 > 12.4. The bigger percentage is not the bigger amount, which is the whole point of the question — and the scheme needs both figures, not just the decision.

html: Simplify m × m × m × m
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2024
subject: Maths
answer: m4 — B1 cao. Four ms multiplied together. The index counts them; it does not multiply them, so it is not 4m.

html:
In a competition, a player gets 5 points for each game they win, 2 points for each game they draw and 0 points for each game they lose.

Amy wins x games and draws y games.

answer: 0.4 — the matching pair is 4 ÷ 10 = 0.4 and 40 ÷ 100 = 0.4; the other two are 40 ÷ 10 = 4 and 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04. Dividing by 100 moves every digit two places to the right, so 40 goes 40 → 4 → 0.4, and the slip to watch for is stopping after one place (4) or carrying on to 0.04.

Of those the only pair two apart is 17 and 19 — 19 and 23 differ by 4, and 17 and 23 by 6. The trap is spotting a difference of 2 first and circling 21 and 23, or 23 and 25: the primes have to be picked out before the difference is looked for.
