html: Match each shape to the correct fraction: 1⁄100, 1⁄4, 2⁄5, 1⁄10
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Equivalent & Simplifying Fractions, Area of 2-D Shapes
examiner_note: The lead says only that W, X, Y and Z cover different fractions of a 10 by 10 square; it does not say how many of the 100 small squares each shape covers, so no shape can be matched to a fraction.

html:
Match the name of each 3-D shape to its number of vertices.

cube, square-based pyramid, triangular-based prism, octagonal-based pyramid — 9, 8, 6, 5
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: cube → 8, square-based pyramid → 5, triangular-based prism → 6, octagonal-based pyramid → 9 — a pyramid has one vertex per corner of its base plus the apex on top, so a square base gives 4 + 1 = 5 and an octagonal base gives 8 + 1 = 9. A prism is two copies of its base joined up, so a triangular prism gives 3 × 2 = 6 and a cube gives 4 × 2 = 8. Each of the four numbers is used once, which is a useful check. The trap is counting faces or edges instead of corners — a cube has 6 faces, and 6 is one of the numbers on offer, so that slip lands on a plausible-looking wrong line.

html:
A class votes for a captain. Three-quarters of the class vote for Sam. The remaining 7 pupils vote for Alex.

How many pupils are in the class?
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 28 — three-quarters vote for Sam, so the 7 who vote for Alex are the remaining quarter. One quarter is 7, so the whole class is 7 × 4 = 28 (check: three-quarters of 28 is 21, and 21 + 7 = 28). The step children miss is that the 7 is the leftover fraction rather than the given fraction; the common wrong answer is 21, which is Sam's share rather than the class.

html:
Write the missing number to make this multiplication correct.

3.207 × 100 =      × 10
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Place Value & Ordering, Calculating with Decimals
answer: 32.07 — the left-hand side is 3.207 × 100 = 320.7, so the box must make box × 10 = 320.7, which gives 320.7 ÷ 10 = 32.07. The quicker route is to compare the two multipliers: 10 is a tenth of 100, so the box has to be ten times 3.207. The trap is writing 320.7 — the value of the left-hand side rather than the number that belongs in the box.

lead: Here is a number: 9,658,214
html:
Tick the statements that are true.

The digit 5 represents 50,000
The value of the digit 9 is nine hundred thousands.
The digit 6 represents 6 millions.
The value of the digit 2 is twenty tens.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Place Value & Ordering, Reading & Writing Numbers
answer: Tick the first and the fourth — 9,658,214 breaks up as 9 millions, 6 hundred thousands, 5 ten thousands, 8 thousands, 2 hundreds, 1 ten and 4 ones. So the 5 does represent 50,000, and the 2 represents 200, which is twenty tens. The other two are each shifted one place and are false: the 9 is worth 9,000,000, not nine hundred thousand, and the 6 is worth 600,000, not 6 millions. The fourth is the one children leave unticked — "twenty tens" is an unfamiliar way of writing 200 rather than a wrong one, so it is worth saying out loud as 20 × 10.

lead: Four shopping items with weights and prices: 670 g at £1.50, 400 g at £0.70, 500 g of butter with no price shown, 750 g at £1.45.
html:
Chen buys these four items. Chen pays for the four items with a £10 note. The price of the butter is not shown. She receives £3.85 change.

What is the price of the butter? Show your method.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: £2.50 — the four items together cost £10 − £3.85 = £6.15. The three priced items come to £1.50 + £0.70 + £1.45 = £3.65. So the butter is £6.15 − £3.65 = £2.50. Both steps are needed for the marks, and the first is the one that gets skipped: children start adding the three prices without first turning the change into a total. The weights — 670 g, 400 g, 500 g, 750 g — are printed to be ignored; nothing here is priced per kilogram.

lead: A scale from 1 to 2 kilograms.
html: Draw an arrow on the scale below to show 1350 grams.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: An arrow pointing at 1.35 kg — 1350 g ÷ 1000 = 1.35 kg, and the scale runs from 1 kg to 2 kg, so that is 0.35 of the way along it, a little over a third past the 1 kg mark. Convert first and place second: the usual slip is to read "350 grams past 1 kilogram" as "halfway towards 1.5" and put the arrow at the middle, and the other is writing 13.5. Exactly which printed division it lands on depends on how the scale is subdivided, which the transcription does not record — but the value the arrow must point at is 1.35 kg either way.

html:
A hall has 1,250 seats. At 7 pm, 880 seats are filled. At 8 pm, there are 40 empty seats.

How many seats were filled between 7 pm and 8 pm? Show your method.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
330 — at 8 pm the only seats not filled are the 40 empty ones, so 1,250 − 40 = 1,210 seats are filled at that point. The hall went from 880 filled to 1,210 filled, so the number filled in that hour is 1,210 − 880 = 330.
The same answer comes the other way round, and it is worth showing a child both: at 7 pm there are 1,250 − 880 = 370 empty seats, and by 8 pm only 40 of those are left, so 370 − 40 = 330 of them were taken.
The hard step is that “40 empty seats” is not a count of anybody — it has to be turned into 1,210 filled before any subtracting happens. The two wrong answers to watch for are 1,210 (found the 8 pm figure and stopped) and 370 (subtracted 880 from 1,250 and forgot the 40). Both are one subtraction short, and both are worth a mark for method on a 2-mark question.

html:
Each day, a school has break from 10:15 am to 10:30 am and lunchtime from 12:40 pm to 1:30 pm.

What is the total time the school has for breaks and lunchtime in a 5-day week? Show your method.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
5 hours 25 minutes — break runs 10:15 to 10:30, which is 15 minutes. Lunchtime runs 12:40 to 1:30 pm: 20 minutes to get up to 1 o’clock, then 30 minutes past it, so 50 minutes.
One day is 15 + 50 = 65 minutes. Five days is 65 × 5 = 325 minutes. Converting back: 325 ÷ 60 = 5 remainder 25, so 5 hours 25 minutes. (325 minutes on its own is the same answer written differently.)
The trap is the lunchtime interval, because it crosses 1 o’clock: written as a column subtraction, 1:30 − 12:40 comes out as 90 minutes rather than 50, and a child using that gets 8 hours 45 for the week. Counting up in two hops — to the hour, then past it — is the method that does not break. The second slip is reading 325 minutes as 3 hours 25.

lead: Four labelled lines AB, CD, EF and GH drawn on the page.
html:
Tick all the correct statements.

AB is parallel to CD
GH is parallel to AB
CD is perpendicular to GH
EF is perpendicular to CD
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
examiner_note: The lead says only that four labelled lines AB, CD, EF and GH are drawn on the page, and gives no direction, angle or position for any of them, so which pairs are parallel and which are perpendicular cannot be worked out from these words.

lead: Table of distances travelled to school. Amina 1.8 km, William 2.4, Layla 3.2, Chen 1.6, Dev 4.5.
html:
This table shows the distance that five friends travel to school each day.

What is the mean distance they travel to school each day? Show your method.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
2.7 km — add the five distances, then divide by 5 because there are five friends.
1.8 + 2.4 + 3.2 + 1.6 + 4.5 = 13.5 km, then 13.5 ÷ 5 = 2.7 km.
The addition is the easy half; the division is where it goes wrong. 13.5 ÷ 5 is done cleanly by partitioning into 10 + 3.5, which gives 2 + 0.7 = 2.7, rather than by trying to share 13.5 in one go. The other standard slip on a mean question is dividing by the wrong number — here there are five names in the table and five distances, so it is 5, and a child who divides by 4 gets 3.375 and should be sent back to count the rows.

html:
Mrs Mills has 940 seeds to plant into trays. She plants 12 seeds in each tray. The last tray is not full.

What fraction of the last tray is filled? Show your method.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
1⁄3 — 940 ÷ 12 = 78 remainder 4, because 78 × 12 = 936 and 940 − 936 = 4.
So 78 trays are filled completely and 4 seeds are left over for the last one. A full tray holds 12, so the last tray holds 4 out of 12: 4⁄12, which simplifies to 1⁄3.
The step that is actually hard is reading the remainder as a fraction — the remainder is the numerator and the number that fills one tray is the denominator. A child who has divided perfectly well and got 78 r 4 will often write the fraction upside down, or write 4⁄78 by pairing the two numbers that are in front of them rather than the two that belong together. Both 4⁄12 and 1⁄3 say the same thing; the simplified form is the safer one to teach.

lead: Here are four numbers: 40, 60, 64, 100
html:
Use each number once to complete these statements.

    is a square number.
    is a cube number.
    is a common multiple of 4 and 5
    is a common factor of 80 and 120
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Squares & Square Roots, Cubes & Cube Roots, Factors & Multiples, HCF & LCM
answer:
100 is a square number, 64 is a cube number, 60 is a common multiple of 4 and 5, 40 is a common factor of 80 and 120 — and the order they are worked out in is the whole question.
Two of the numbers are square: 64 = 8 × 8 and 100 = 10 × 10. Only one is a cube: 64 = 4 × 4 × 4. So the cube line has to take 64, and that leaves 100 for the square line.
Then three of them are multiples of both 4 and 5: 40, 60 and 100 are all multiples of 20. But 100 is already used, and the last line needs a number that divides into 80 and 120. 80 ÷ 40 = 2 and 120 ÷ 40 = 3, so 40 works; 60 does not go into 80 at all. So 40 takes the common-factor line and 60 is left for the common-multiple line.
The trap is filling the square line first with 64, which looks right and leaves nothing for the cube. Teach it as: find the line that has only one possible answer and start there. The other place it goes wrong is confusing multiple and factor on the last two lines — a multiple is bigger than 4 and 5, a factor is smaller than 80 and 120.

lead: A table with columns a and b. One row has a = 2, another has b = 13.
html: Write the missing numbers so that 3 × b − a = 2
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
examiner_note: The two values the lead gives do not fit the equation as transcribed: with a = 2, 3 x b - a = 2 gives b = 1 and one third, which cannot be a missing number in this table, so either the equation or which column holds 2 and which holds 13 has not come across correctly and the answers cannot be settled from these words.

html:
Here are 3 translations on a coordinate grid. Tick the translations that are four units to the left.

from (0, 2) to (4, 2)
from (6, 8) to (2, 8)
from (−3, 5) to (−7, 5)
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer:
The second and third — (6, 8) to (2, 8) and (−3, 5) to (−7, 5).
Four units to the left means the x coordinate goes down by 4 and the y coordinate does not change at all. 6 − 4 = 2, so the second one is a move of four left; −3 − 4 = −7, so the third one is too. The first goes from x = 0 to x = 4, which is four units to the right, so it is not ticked. The y value stays the same in all three, so it settles nothing here.
The one that catches children is the third. Going left from −3 lands on −7, and a child who compares the digits rather than the numbers reads −7 as bigger than −3 and calls it a move to the right. Counting back along a number line through zero — −3, −4, −5, −6, −7 — is what makes it obvious, and it is worth doing out loud rather than in a head.

html:
Olivia has two jars of beads. The number of beads in Jar A is double the number of beads in Jar B.

Olivia says, “25% of the number of beads in Jar A is the same as 50% of the number of beads in Jar B.”

Explain why Olivia is correct.
name: Paper 2: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Percentage of an Amount, Ratio Problems
answer:
Because Jar A holds twice as many beads as Jar B, taking 25% of A is taking a quarter of two lots of B, and a quarter of two lots is a half of one lot — so 25% of A = 25% of (2 × B) = 50% of B.
With numbers: if Jar B has 10 beads then Jar A has 20. 25% of 20 = 5, and 50% of 10 = 5. The same works for any pair — B = 40 and A = 80 gives 20 either way.
A worked example earns the mark just as well as the algebra here, and it is the safer thing to teach. But the explanation has to say why: “they are both 5” on its own is not an explanation, and that is where the mark is usually lost. The sentence needs the words “because Jar A is double Jar B” in it — the doubling is exactly what cancels out the halving of the percentage.

lead: Circles and rectangles with fractions shaded. One match has been done already.
html:
These shapes have a fraction shaded.

Match each shaded fraction of a circle to the same shaded fraction of a rectangle.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
examiner_note: The lead says only that circles and rectangles have fractions shaded — it never says which fraction each individual shape shows, so there is nothing to match one against another.

html:
The temperature in a freezer is −40 °C. The temperature increases by 10 °C.

What is the new temperature?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: −30 °C — an increase means counting forwards along the number line, so ten steps up from −40 lands on −30. The standard trap is to treat “add 10” as making the number bigger in the sense of further from zero and answer −50; drawing a line with 0 marked on it and walking the ten steps towards zero settles it every time.

lead: Milk priced £1.45 and orange juice priced £2.40.
html:
Jack buys milk and orange juice from a shop. He pays with a £5 note.

How much change does Jack get? Show your method.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: £1.15 — the two items first: £1.45 + £2.40 = £3.85. Then the change: £5.00 − £3.85 = £1.15. This is worth 2 marks and the paper asks for the method, so both lines have to be written down — a bare £1.15 with no working throws a mark away even though it is right. The subtraction is the step to slow down on: counting on is easier than borrowing here, £3.85 → £4.00 is 15p and £4.00 → £5.00 is £1, giving £1.15.

html:
The diameter of the Moon is 3,476 kilometres.

What is this diameter to the nearest hundred kilometres?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 3,500 km — to round to the nearest hundred, look at what follows the hundreds digit: 3,476, and 76 is more than 50, so the 4 hundreds go up to 5 hundreds and everything after becomes zero. The usual error is to look at the final digit instead and round to the nearest ten, answering 3,480.

lead: One has been done for you.
html:
Match each of these Roman numerals to the correct number.

CVI  DXC  DLXXI  MCX — 1110, 106, 590, 571
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: CVI = 106, DXC = 590, DLXXI = 571, MCX = 1110 — read left to right adding the letters, except where a smaller letter sits before a larger one, which means subtract. CVI is 100 + 5 + 1. DLXXI is 500 + 50 + 10 + 10 + 1 = 571. MCX is 1,000 + 100 + 10 = 1,110. DXC is the one that catches children out: the XC is 100 − 10 = 90, so it is 500 + 90 = 590, not 500 + 10 + 100. Once DXC is placed the other three follow, because 571 is the only other number in the 500s.

lead: One has been done for you.
html:
Match each fraction to its equivalent simplified fraction.

12⁄20  12⁄15  12⁄16  12⁄18 — 4⁄5, 2⁄3, 3⁄5, 3⁄4
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 12⁄20 = 3⁄5, 12⁄15 = 4⁄5, 12⁄16 = 3⁄4, 12⁄18 = 2⁄3 — divide top and bottom by the highest common factor each time, which is 4, 3, 4 and 6 respectively. Because every numerator is the same 12, the whole question is really about the denominator: whatever you divide 12 by, you must divide the bottom by as well. The two fifths are the pair to separate carefully — 12⁄20 is the smaller fraction, so it is 3⁄5, and 12⁄15 is 4⁄5.

html:
Emma thinks of a number. She says, “multiply by 2, add 11, divide by 3. My answer is 9”

What number did Emma think of?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 8 — work backwards, undoing each instruction in reverse order: 9 × 3 = 27, then 27 − 11 = 16, then 16 ÷ 2 = 8. The hard part is the order, not the arithmetic: the last thing Emma did is the first thing to undo, and a child who correctly flips each operation but keeps the original order (÷ 2 first) gets nowhere. Always check forwards: 8 × 2 = 16, 16 + 11 = 27, 27 ÷ 3 = 9.

lead: A shape drawn on a coordinate grid, x from -7 to 7 and y from 0 to 8.
html:
Here is a shape.

Draw the shape after it is translated 8 units to the right. Use a ruler.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
examiner_note: The lead gives the grid's axes but not where the shape's vertices sit on it, so there is no starting position to move 8 units right from.

lead: Table of weeks to days. 1 week 7 days, 2 weeks 14 days, 4 weeks 28 days, 6 weeks blank, 10 weeks blank, blank weeks 105 days.
html: Write the missing numbers in the table.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 42 days, 70 days and 15 weeks — every row is weeks × 7, so 6 × 7 = 42 and 10 × 7 = 70. The last row is the one worth slowing down for, because it runs the other way: 105 days is the answer already given and the weeks are missing, so divide — 105 ÷ 7 = 15 weeks. A child on autopilot multiplies and writes 735.

lead: A quadrilateral ABCD printed on the page.
html: What is the perimeter of the shape, in millimetres? Use a ruler.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
examiner_note: The row describes a quadrilateral ABCD printed on the page but gives none of its side lengths, and the perimeter is obtained by measuring that printed figure with a ruler.

html: Measure the size of angle d. Use an angle measurer.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
examiner_note: Nothing in the row says how big angle d is or where its arms lie - it is read off the printed figure with an angle measurer.

html:
Write the missing digits to make this subtraction correct.

  □ 5 7
− 3 □ 5
    6 8
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
examiner_note: The column subtraction has been flattened onto one line, and the digits as transcribed form no valid subtraction under any grouping, so which digits belong to the top number, the number subtracted and the answer cannot be recovered.

html:
Here are four fractions.

7⁄8  1⁄5  3⁄4  8⁄10

Write the fractions in order starting with the least.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub>, <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>4</sub>, <sup>8</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub>, <sup>7</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> — over a common denominator of 40 they are <sup>8</sup>⁄<sub>40</sub>, <sup>30</sup>⁄<sub>40</sub>, <sup>32</sup>⁄<sub>40</sub> and <sup>35</sup>⁄<sub>40</sub>, so that is the order. As decimals: 0.2, 0.75, 0.8, 0.875. <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> is the only one under a half and goes first on sight; the hard pair is <sup>8</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> against <sup>7</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub>, and the standard trap is to put <sup>8</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> last because both its numbers are bigger — it is the smaller of the two, because <sup>7</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> is only <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> short of 1 while <sup>8</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> is <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> short.

lead: Four box sizes on a truck: 6 boxes at 4 kg, 2 boxes at 6.5 kg, 8 boxes at 13 kg, 4 boxes at 2.5 kg.
html:
There are 20 boxes on a truck. The boxes are in 4 different sizes.

What is the total mass of the 20 boxes on the truck? Show your method.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 151 kg — 6 × 4 = 24, 2 × 6.5 = 13, 8 × 13 = 104 and 4 × 2.5 = 10, then 24 + 13 + 104 + 10 = 151. The first move is to check 6 + 2 + 8 + 4 = 20, which confirms every box on the truck is accounted for once. The step worth slowing down on is 8 × 13, since those eight boxes are more than two-thirds of the load — 8 × 10 = 80 and 8 × 3 = 24, so 104. The two decimal rows are easier than they look: 2 × 6.5 is double 6.5, and 4 × 2.5 is four quarters of ten.

lead: Table of labels and percentages: A 20%, B 25%, C 15%, D 30%, E 10%. A partly completed pie chart showing A and B.
html:
Look at the data in this table.

Using this data, draw two lines and write three labels to complete the pie chart. Use a ruler.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Pie Charts, Percentage of an Amount
answer: Two more lines from the centre, cutting the space left into sectors of 54° for C, 108° for D and 36° for E, each labelled — A (20%) and B (25%) are already drawn and take 72° + 90° = 162°, leaving 360° − 162° = 198°. Every percentage is worth 3.6°, so 15 × 3.6 = 54, 30 × 3.6 = 108 and 10 × 3.6 = 36, and 54 + 108 + 36 = 198 is the check to do before touching the ruler. If the printed circle is already divided into twenty equal parts, count parts instead of degrees: one part is 5%, so C is 3 parts, D is 6 and E is 2. The sizes are fixed by the data; which of the three sits next to B is not, so the labels must be written to match whatever the two lines actually cut.

html:
35% of the 680 pupils at a school have a pet dog. 159 of the pupils who have a pet dog are boys.

How many of the pupils who have a pet dog are girls? Show your method.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 79 — 35% of 680 is 238: 10% is 68, so 30% is 204, and 5% is half of 68, which is 34; 204 + 34 = 238. Then 238 − 159 = 79 girls. The arithmetic is not the hard part — the trap is stopping at 238, which is the number of pupils with a dog rather than the number asked for. Reading the last line back (“how many are girls”) before writing the answer is what earns the second mark.

html:
Write a number in the box to make this correct.

3⁄5 <   ⁄100 < 0.7
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Fraction Decimal Percentage Conversion, Ordering Fractions
answer: Any whole number from 61 to 69 — 65 is the tidiest to write. Put everything over 100: <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> = <sup>60</sup>⁄<sub>100</sub> and 0.7 = <sup>70</sup>⁄<sub>100</sub>, so the box has to sit strictly between 60 and 70. Both signs are < and not ≤, so 60 and 70 are wrong — that is the whole of the question, and the two ends are the only answers a child is likely to offer.

html:
Tick the numbers that are factors of both 54 and 72

2  3  4  8  9
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 2, 3 and 9 — 54 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 and 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3, so the highest common factor is 2 × 3 × 3 = 18, and every common factor is a factor of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. From the list offered that is 2, 3 and 9. The trap is 4 and 8, which both divide 72 and neither divides 54 — 54 ÷ 4 = 13.5 and 54 ÷ 8 = 6.75 — so a child who checks only against 72 ticks five numbers instead of three. Checking the smaller number first is the habit worth teaching here.

html:
Layla wants to buy a camera that costs £65. For the first 10 weeks, she saves £2 each week. Then she saves £3 each week.

How many weeks altogether does it take Layla to save £65? Show your method.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 25 weeks — the first 10 weeks bring in 10 × £2 = £20, so £65 − £20 = £45 is still to find. At £3 a week that takes £45 ÷ £3 = 15 more weeks, and 10 + 15 = 25 weeks altogether. Two marks, so both stages have to be shown. The trap is stopping at 15 — the question asks how many weeks altogether, not how many weeks at £3.

html:
Complete this division.

    □ 6 □ 4 r1
12 ) □ 4 3 □ 6
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
examiner_note: The transcribed division cannot be right — 12 × any whole number is even, so a dividend ending in 6 can never leave a remainder of 1 — which means one of the printed characters has been mis-read, and the two ways of repairing it give different dividends (44,329 ÷ 12 = 3,694 r 1, or 44,336 ÷ 12 = 3,694 r 8), so the boxes cannot be filled with certainty.

lead: Four shapes A, B, C and D drawn on a grid.
html: Write the letters of all the shapes that have only two acute angles.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
examiner_note: The row says only that four shapes A, B, C and D are drawn on a grid and never says what any of them is, so there is nothing here from which to count acute angles.

html:
A band holds a concert for charity. The tickets cost £27 each. They sell 635 tickets. They pay £3,180 to use the hall. They give one-third of the remaining amount to charity.

How much money does the band give to charity? Show your method.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
topics: Long Multiplication, Subtraction, Fractions of an Amount
answer: £4,655 — the ticket money is 635 × £27 = £17,145 (635 × 20 = 12,700 and 635 × 7 = 4,445, added). Take off the hall: £17,145 − £3,180 = £13,965. One third of what is left is £13,965 ÷ 3 = £4,655. Three marks, so the long multiplication and the division both belong on the page. The step children lose is the order — the hall comes out before the third is taken, and answering £13,965 or £5,715 (a third of the £17,145) is the usual slip.

lead: Sarah makes jewellery using black and white beads. black = (white x 3) + 4
html: Sarah uses 12 white beads to make a necklace. How many black beads does she use?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 40 — the rule is black = (white × 3) + 4, so with 12 white beads it is 12 × 3 = 36, then 36 + 4 = 40 black beads. Straight substitution; the only slip is adding the 4 first.

html: Sarah uses 25 black beads to make a bracelet. How many white beads does she use?
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: 7 — this one runs the rule backwards: 25 − 4 = 21, then 21 ÷ 3 = 7 white beads. Check it forwards: 7 × 3 = 21, + 4 = 25. ✓ The hard part is that the two steps must be undone in the reverse order — dividing by 3 first gives 8 remainder 1 and reads as if the rule has broken.

lead: Table with rows cube, pentagonal prism, triangular-based pyramid and a column for number of faces.
html: Complete the table.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Cube 6, pentagonal prism 7, triangular-based pyramid 4 — a pentagonal prism has a pentagon at each end plus one rectangle for each of the pentagon's five sides, so 2 + 5 = 7. A triangular-based pyramid has the triangular base plus three sloping triangles, so 4. The two things that go wrong are counting edges instead of faces, and reading “triangular” or “pentagonal” as the answer — the word names the end face, not the total.

html:
1⁄2 × 5⁄6 is greater than the value of 1⁄3 × 7⁄8

Explain how you know.
name: Paper 3: Reasoning — May 2024
subject: Maths
answer: Because ½ × 5⁄6 = 5⁄12 = 10⁄24 and 1⁄3 × 7⁄8 = 7⁄24, and 10⁄24 is greater than 7⁄24. A version that needs no common denominator also earns it: 5⁄12 is more than 4⁄12 = 1⁄3, while multiplying 1⁄3 by 7⁄8 (less than 1) makes it smaller than 1⁄3 — so one is above a third and the other below it. Worth saying to a child: the tempting “both fractions are bigger” argument is false here, because 5⁄6 is less than 7⁄8; it is the ½ against the 1⁄3 that decides it.

The two objectives are marked separately and added. A response that is off the task earns nothing for AO5 and can still earn AO6.

html: 2⁄3  +  1⁄6
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 5⁄6 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 6 is the smallest number both 3 and 6 divide into, so it becomes 4⁄6 + 1⁄6 = 5⁄6.

html: 3⁄8  −  1⁄4
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄8 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be subtracted. 8 is the smallest number both 8 and 4 divide into, so it becomes 3⁄8 − 2⁄8 = 1⁄8.

html: 7⁄20  +  2⁄5
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 3⁄4 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 20 is the smallest number both 20 and 5 divide into, so it becomes 7⁄20 + 8⁄20 = 15⁄20. 15⁄20 cancels down to 3⁄4.

html: 11⁄18  +  1⁄6
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 7⁄9 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 18 is the smallest number both 18 and 6 divide into, so it becomes 11⁄18 + 3⁄18 = 14⁄18. 14⁄18 cancels down to 7⁄9.

html: 7⁄15  −  1⁄5
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 4⁄15 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be subtracted. 15 is the smallest number both 15 and 5 divide into, so it becomes 7⁄15 − 3⁄15 = 4⁄15.

html: 39⁄100  −  7⁄20
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 1⁄25 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be subtracted. 100 is the smallest number both 100 and 20 divide into, so it becomes 39⁄100 − 35⁄100 = 4⁄100. 4⁄100 cancels down to 1⁄25.

html: 1⁄2  +  2⁄5
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 9⁄10 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 10 is the smallest number both 2 and 5 divide into, so it becomes 5⁄10 + 4⁄10 = 9⁄10.

html: 1⁄3  +  1⁄2
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 5⁄6 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 6 is the smallest number both 3 and 2 divide into, so it becomes 2⁄6 + 3⁄6 = 5⁄6.

html: 4⁄5  −  2⁄3
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 2⁄15 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be subtracted. 15 is the smallest number both 5 and 3 divide into, so it becomes 12⁄15 − 10⁄15 = 2⁄15.

html: 5⁄11  +  1⁄4
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 31⁄44 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 44 is the smallest number both 11 and 4 divide into, so it becomes 20⁄44 + 11⁄44 = 31⁄44.

html: 3⁄4  −  2⁄5
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 7⁄20 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be subtracted. 20 is the smallest number both 4 and 5 divide into, so it becomes 15⁄20 − 8⁄20 = 7⁄20.

html: 8⁄9  −  3⁄5
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 13⁄45 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be subtracted. 45 is the smallest number both 9 and 5 divide into, so it becomes 40⁄45 − 27⁄45 = 13⁄45.

html: What fraction of the cars in the car park are red or blue?
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>2</sub> of the cars in a car park are red. <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>4</sub> of the cars in the car park are blue.
answer: 3⁄4 — halves and quarters do not add until they are the same thing, and a half IS 2⁄4. So it is 2 + 1 = 3 quarters.

html: What fraction of his pocket money has Harry spent?
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: This week Harry spent <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> of his pocket money on a ticket for a match. He also spent <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> of his pocket money on a scarf at the match.
answer: 7⁄9 — ninths are already thirds cut smaller, so only the first fraction moves: 2⁄3 is 6⁄9, and 6 + 1 = 7 ninths.

html: What fraction of the counters are blue?
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: In a bag, there are green, white and blue counters. <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> of the counters are green. <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> of the counters are white.
answer: 3⁄10 — there are only three colours, so they make one whole between them. Green and white are 1⁄10 + 6⁄10 = 7⁄10, and 10⁄10 − 7⁄10 = 3⁄10, which cancels to 3⁄10.

html: What fraction of the rectangle is not shaded?
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: A rectangle is split into three parts: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> of it is shaded pink and <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> of it is shaded blue. The rest is left white.
answer: 7⁄15 — add the shaded parts first: fifteenths take both, so 5⁄15 + 3⁄15 = 8⁄15. Then the whole rectangle is 15⁄15, and 15⁄15 − 8⁄15 = 7⁄15. Answering 8⁄15 is the usual slip — that is the part that IS shaded.

html: What fraction of the children study Italian?
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: In Year 7, the children study one language. They study French, German or Italian. <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> of the children study French. <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>6</sub> of the children study German.
answer: 11⁄24 — “one language” each is what makes the three add to one whole. 24 is the smallest number 8 and 6 both divide into: 9⁄24 + 4⁄24 = 13⁄24, and 24⁄24 − 13⁄24 = 11⁄24.

html: Work out the fraction of the park that is the picnic area
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: A park is divided into a play area, a tennis court and a picnic area. The play area is <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> of the park and the tennis court is <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> of it.
answer: 8⁄45 — the three parts are the whole park. 45 is the smallest number 5 and 9 both divide into: 27⁄45 + 10⁄45 = 37⁄45, and 45⁄45 − 37⁄45 = 8⁄45.

html: How much orange juice did Yasmin pour out?
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: Yasmin has a bottle that contains <sup>7</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> litre of orange juice. She pours out some orange juice and now has <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>4</sub> litre left.
answer: 9⁄20 litre — what was poured out is what has gone: 7⁄10 − 1⁄4. Twentieths take both, so 14⁄20 − 5⁄20 = 9⁄20.

html: 1⁄3  +  1⁄5  +  1⁄10
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 19⁄30 — three at once is no different from two: find one bottom they all divide into, which is 30, and add the tops. 10⁄30 + 6⁄30 + 3⁄30 = 19⁄30, and 19 is prime, so nothing cancels.

html: 3⁄4  +  11⁄12
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 12⁄3 — the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 12 is the smallest number both 4 and 12 divide into, so it becomes 9⁄12 + 11⁄12 = 20⁄12. That is more than one whole, so it is written 12⁄3.

html: 11⁄3  −  1⁄2
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 5⁄6 — turn the mixed number into 4⁄3 first, then the bottoms have to match before the tops can be subtracted. 6 is the smallest number both 3 and 2 divide into, so it becomes 8⁄6 − 3⁄6 = 5⁄6.

html: 21⁄4  +  5⁄8
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 27⁄8 — turn the mixed number into 9⁄4 first, then the bottoms have to match before the tops can be added. 8 is the smallest number both 4 and 8 divide into, so it becomes 18⁄8 + 5⁄8 = 23⁄8. That is more than one whole, so it is written 27⁄8.

name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
html: 52⁄5  −  18⁄9
answer: 323⁄45 — turn both mixed numbers top-heavy first, then the bottoms have to match before the tops can be subtracted. 45 is the smallest number both 5 and 9 divide into, so it becomes 243⁄45 − 85⁄45 = 158⁄45. That is more than one whole, so it is written 323⁄45.

html: Write the missing numbers
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: The numbers in this sequence increase by the same amount each time: ◻, 1<sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>2</sub>, 2<sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>, 3<sup>5</sup>⁄<sub>6</sub>, ◻
answer: 1⁄3 and 5 — find the step first, from two terms you have been given: 22⁄3 − 11⁄2 is 16⁄6 − 9⁄6 = 7⁄6, which is 11⁄6. Then go one step back from 11⁄2 and one step on from 35⁄6. The second one comes out as a whole number, which is the part that looks wrong and is not.

html: Work out the distance from Antrim to Randalstown
name: Adding Fractions: Different Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: Kayleigh is walking from Antrim to Randalstown. She passes a signpost. One arm points back the way she came: Antrim 3<sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> miles. The other arm points on: Randalstown 1<sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>4</sub> miles, Toome 9<sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>4</sub> miles.
answer: 51⁄12 miles — the signpost splits the walk in two at the post, so the whole journey is the bit behind her plus the bit ahead: 31⁄3 + 13⁄4. Twelfths take both: 40⁄12 + 21⁄12 = 61⁄12, which is 51⁄12. Toome is on the sign to be ignored — it is further down the same road and she is not going there.

html: 2⁄5  +  1⁄5
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 3⁄5 — the denominators already match, so the bottom stays where it is and only the tops are added: 2 + 1 = 3, over 5.

html: 7⁄9  −  5⁄9
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 2⁄9 — the denominators already match, so the bottom stays where it is and only the tops are subtracted: 7 − 5 = 2, over 9.

html: 6⁄11  +  2⁄11
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 8⁄11 — the denominators already match, so the bottom stays where it is and only the tops are added: 6 + 2 = 8, over 11.

html: 16⁄25  −  4⁄25
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 12⁄25 — the denominators already match, so the bottom stays where it is and only the tops are subtracted: 16 − 4 = 12, over 25.

html: 2⁄3  +  2⁄3
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 11⁄3 — the denominators already match, so the bottom stays where it is and only the tops are added: 2 + 2 = 4, over 3. That is more than one whole, so it is written 11⁄3.

html: 3⁄8  +  7⁄8
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
answer: 11⁄4 — the denominators already match, so the bottom stays where it is and only the tops are added: 3 + 7 = 10, over 8. That is more than one whole, so it is written 11⁄4.

html: What fraction of the cupcakes in the box are lemon or strawberry?
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>12</sub> of the cupcakes in a box are lemon. <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>12</sub> of the cupcakes in the box are strawberry.
answer: 5⁄12 — “or” means put the two groups together, so add them: 1 + 4 = 5 twelfths. It does not cancel, because 5 and 12 share no factor.

html: What fraction of the class are right handed?
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> of the students in a class are left handed.
answer: 2⁄3 — everybody is one or the other, so the whole class is 1, which is 3⁄3. Take away the left handers: 3 − 1 = 2 thirds.

html: In total, how much of the cake has Kenneth eaten?
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: On Monday, Kenneth ate <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> of a cake. On Tuesday he ate <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>8</sub> of the same cake.
answer: 5⁄8 — “in total” is an add: 2 + 3 = 5 eighths. It is the same cake both days, which is what lets the eighths be added at all.

html: What fraction of the matches did they lose?
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: In one season, a netball team won <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> of their matches. They drew <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> of their matches.
answer: 1⁄3 — a match is won, drawn or lost and nothing else, so the three make one whole. Won and drawn together are 4 + 2 = 6 ninths, and 9⁄9 − 6⁄9 = 3⁄9, which cancels to 1⁄3.

html: What fraction of the children study French?
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: In a school, the children study French, German or Spanish. <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>7</sub> of the children study Spanish. Half of the remaining children study French.
answer: 3⁄7 — the trap is “half”, which is half of what is LEFT and not half of the school. Spanish takes 1⁄7, leaving 6⁄7, and half of six sevenths is three sevenths.

html: Find the distance from the hotel to the shop
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: A straight road runs Beach — Hotel — Shop. It is <sup>11</sup>⁄<sub>12</sub> km from the beach to the shop, and <sup>5</sup>⁄<sub>12</sub> km from the beach to the hotel.
answer: 1⁄2 km — the hotel is on the way, so the short hop is the whole road minus the first part: 11 − 5 = 6 twelfths, and 6⁄12 cancels to 1⁄2.

html: Write down three fractions that may have been added together
name: Adding Fractions: Same Denominators
subject: Maths
lead: Three different fractions have been added together and the answer is <sup>17</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub>.
answer: Several work, and <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub> + <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> + <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>2</sub> is the neatest — the quickest route is to split 17 into three different numbers of twentieths, say 1 + 6 + 10, and then cancel each one down. Anything that adds to <sup>17</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub> is right, so check yours by putting it over 20.

name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18 — in pairs: 1 × 18, 2 × 9, 3 × 6. The next try is 4 (no) then 5 (no), and by then the pairs have met in the middle, which is how you know to stop.

name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 1, 5, 25 — only three, because 25 is a square number: 1 × 25 and 5 × 5. A square always has an odd number of factors, since one pair is a number with itself.

name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 20, 40 — in pairs: 1 × 40, 2 × 20, 4 × 10, 5 × 8. Eight of them, and 3, 6, 7 and 9 all fail.

html: Here is a list of numbers. 3 4 5 6 7 9 13 From the list, write down a factor of 14 From the list, write down a factor of 26
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 7 for 14, and 13 for 26 — 14 = 2 × 7 and 26 = 2 × 13, and 7 and 13 are the only numbers on the list that go into them. 2 would work for both and is not on the list, which is the point of the question.

html: Here is a list of numbers. 4 5 6 7 8 10 12 13 14 Circle any number in the list that is a factor of 24
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 4, 6, 8, 12 — 24 = 4 × 6 = 8 × 3 = 12 × 2. From the list, 5, 7, 10, 13 and 14 all leave a remainder. 14 is the tempting one: 24 is even and 14 is even, but even does not mean it divides.

html: Write three factors of 40 which are also factors of 30
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: Any three of 1, 2, 5, 10 — these are the four numbers that divide BOTH 40 and 30, and a quick way to find them all at once is that they are exactly the factors of 10, the highest common factor. Any three of the four earns the mark.

html: Write all the factors of 36 which are also factors of 27 …………………………………………………………………………………
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 1, 3, 9 — all of them this time, not a choice. They are the factors of 9, which is the highest common factor of 36 and 27. Note what changed from the question before: "write all" means the complete list, so leaving out the 1 loses it.

html: Write four factors of 48 that are not factors of 30
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: Any four of 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48 — 48 has factors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48 and 30 has 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30, so knock out the ones they share (1, 2, 3, 6) and six are left. Any four of those six.

html: Jemima has 32 sweets and is able to share them equally between her friends. Jemima has more than 5 friends but less than 20 friends. Write down how many friends Jemima might have.
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 8 or 16 — sharing 32 equally means the number of friends is a factor of 32: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. More than 5 and fewer than 20 leaves 8 and 16. Both are right, so either earns it — the question says "might have".

html: 3 5 10 12 25 Shannon writes down three different factors of 36 She adds her three numbers together. The answer is greater than 30 but less than 35. What three numbers could Shannon have written down?
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: Several work, and 4, 12, 18 is the neatest — the factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36, and you want three DIFFERENT ones adding to between 31 and 34. Start from the big ones: 18 has to be in it, because without it the three largest left are 12 + 9 + 6 = 27, short of 31. Then 12 + 18 = 30 needs 1, 2, 3 or 4 alongside, and 9 + 18 = 27 needs 4 or 6. The full set is 1+12+18, 2+12+18, 3+12+18, 4+12+18, 4+9+18 and 6+9+18.

html: Write all the numbers between 12 and 50 that are factors of 90 …………………………………………………………………………………
name: Factors
subject: Maths
answer: 15, 18, 30, 45 — the factors of 90 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 15, 18, 30, 45, 90, and "between 12 and 50" keeps four of them. Watch both ends: 10 is below 12 and 90 is above 50, and neither counts.

name: Accumulation
subject: English Language
description: Piling up words or points one after another for force. “He was rude, loud, careless, cruel.”

name: Adynaton
subject: English Language
description: Hyperbole so extreme it says something is impossible. “When pigs fly.”

name: Allegory
subject: English Language
description: A story whose characters and events stand for something else — usually a moral or political idea.

name: Alliteration
subject: English Language
description: The same sound starting words close together. “The slow, sad song.”

name: Allusion
subject: English Language
description: A passing reference to something outside the text — a book, a myth, an event — without explaining it.

name: Amblysia
subject: English Language
description: Softening bad news before delivering it.

name: Amphiboly
subject: English Language
description: A sentence that can be read two ways because of how it is built, not because of a word’s meaning.

name: Anachronism
subject: English Language
description: Something in the wrong time period — a clock in a Roman play.

name: Anacoluthon
subject: English Language
description: A sentence that starts one way and finishes another, as speech often does.

name: Anadiplosis
subject: English Language
description: Ending a clause and starting the next with the same word. “Fear leads to anger, anger leads to hate.”

name: Analogue
subject: English Language
description: A thing that corresponds to another — a parallel drawn between two situations.

name: Anaphora
subject: English Language
description: The same words at the start of each line or clause. “We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight…”

name: Anastrophe
subject: English Language
description: Words put in an unusual order for effect. “Powerful you have become.”

name: Anecdote
subject: English Language
description: A short personal story used to make a point.

name: Anesis
subject: English Language
description: Ending with a detail that undercuts everything said before it.

name: Antagonist
subject: English Language
description: The character working against the protagonist.

name: Antanaclasis
subject: English Language
description: Repeating a word with a different meaning each time. “Put out the light, then put out the light.”

name: Anthropomorphism
subject: English Language
description: Giving an animal or object a human body or human behaviour — not just human feelings.

name: Anthimeria
subject: English Language
description: Using one part of speech as another. “I’ll text you” — a noun made a verb.

name: Antipophora
subject: English Language
description: Asking a question and immediately answering it yourself.

name: Antimetabole
subject: English Language
description: Repeating a phrase with the order reversed. “Ask not what your country can do for you…”

name: Antiphrasis
subject: English Language
description: Using a word to mean its opposite, usually sarcastically. Calling a giant “Tiny”.

name: Antithesis
subject: English Language
description: Two opposite ideas set against each other in a balanced way. “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.”

name: Antonomasia
subject: English Language
description: Replacing a name with a description, or a description with a name. “The Bard” for Shakespeare.

name: Aphorism
subject: English Language
description: A short statement of a general truth. “Less is more.”

name: Aposiopesis
subject: English Language
description: Breaking off mid-sentence, leaving it unfinished. “If you don’t stop —”

name: Apostrophe
subject: English Language
description: Speaking directly to somebody absent, dead, or to an idea. “O Death, where is thy sting?”

name: Archaism
subject: English Language
description: An old-fashioned word or form used on purpose. “Thou”, “hither”.

name: Assonance
subject: English Language
description: The same vowel sound repeated in nearby words. “The rain in Spain.”

name: Asyndeton
subject: English Language
description: Leaving out the conjunctions to speed a list up. “I came, I saw, I conquered.”

name: Aside
subject: English Language
description: A remark to the audience the other characters cannot hear.

name: Bathos
subject: English Language
description: A sudden drop from the lofty to the ridiculous, usually by accident.

name: Black comedy
subject: English Language
description: Finding humour in things normally too grim to laugh at.

name: Blank verse
subject: English Language
description: Unrhymed lines in iambic pentameter — the usual line of Shakespeare’s plays.

name: Blazon
subject: English Language
description: Listing a person’s features one by one in praise, common in love poetry.

name: Bombast
subject: English Language
description: Language far grander than the subject deserves.

name: Burlesque
subject: English Language
description: Mocking something by treating a serious subject lightly, or a trivial one seriously.

name: Cacophony
subject: English Language
description: Harsh, clashing sounds put together on purpose.

name: Caesura
subject: English Language
description: A deliberate pause in the middle of a line of verse.

name: Catachresis
subject: English Language
description: A word used wrongly or a strained metaphor. “To take arms against a sea of troubles.”

name: Catalexis
subject: English Language
description: Dropping a syllable from the end of a line of verse.

name: Catharsis
subject: English Language
description: The release of emotion an audience feels at the end of a tragedy.

name: Chiasmus
subject: English Language
description: Ideas mirrored in an ABBA order. “Fair is foul, and foul is fair.”

name: Circumlocution
subject: English Language
description: Taking many words to say what could be said in few.

name: Cliché
subject: English Language
description: A phrase worn out by overuse. “At the end of the day.”

name: Conceit
subject: English Language
description: An extended, surprising comparison held across a whole poem.

name: Connotation
subject: English Language
description: What a word suggests beyond its plain meaning — “home” against “house”.

name: Consonance
subject: English Language
description: The same consonant sounds repeated, usually at the ends of words. “pitter patter”.

name: Couplet
subject: English Language
description: Two lines together, usually rhyming.

name: Cyclical ending
subject: English Language
description: An ending that returns to where the piece began.

name: Call to Action
subject: English Language
description: A direct instruction to the reader to do something. Common at the end of persuasive writing.

name: Defamiliarisation
subject: English Language
description: Describing an ordinary thing strangely so it is noticed again.

name: Denotation
subject: English Language
description: A word’s plain dictionary meaning, with nothing suggested on top.

name: Depitation
subject: English Language
description: Cutting a word short by removing its ending.

name: Dissonance
subject: English Language
description: Deliberately awkward, unmusical sound.

name: Double entendre
subject: English Language
description: A phrase with two meanings, one of them usually rude.

name: Dramatic irony
subject: English Language
description: The audience knows something a character does not.

name: Dysphemism
subject: English Language
description: A harsher word used where a neutral one would do — the opposite of a euphemism.

name: Direct Mode of address
subject: English Language
description: Speaking straight to the reader as “you”.

name: Ecphonema
subject: English Language
description: An exclamation — a sudden cry of emotion.

name: Ekphrasis
subject: English Language
description: A vivid description of a work of art inside a piece of writing.

name: Elegy
subject: English Language
description: A poem of mourning for somebody who has died.

name: Elision
subject: English Language
description: Leaving a sound out, usually to fit a rhythm. “o’er” for “over”.

name: Ellipsis
subject: English Language
description: Leaving words out, or the three dots that show it.

name: Emotive language
subject: English Language
description: Word choices picked to stir feeling rather than to inform.

name: Enjambment
subject: English Language
description: A sentence running over the end of a line of verse without a pause.

name: Epanados
subject: English Language
description: Repeating an idea in reverse order to expand on it.

name: Epanalepsis
subject: English Language
description: Beginning and ending a clause with the same word. “The king is dead, long live the king.”

name: Epexegesis
subject: English Language
description: Adding words to make an earlier phrase clearer.

name: Epideictic oratory
subject: English Language
description: Speech of praise or blame — a eulogy, a tribute.

name: Epistrophe
subject: English Language
description: The same word ending each clause — the opposite of anaphora.

name: Epitasis
subject: English Language
description: The part of a play where the action builds toward its climax.

name: Epizeuxis
subject: English Language
description: The same word repeated immediately, with nothing between. “Never, never, never.”

name: Euphemism
subject: English Language
description: A gentler phrase for something harsh. “Passed away.”

name: Euphony
subject: English Language
description: Sounds chosen because they are pleasant together.

name: Farce
subject: English Language
description: Comedy built on absurd situations and improbable coincidence.

name: Feminine rhyme
subject: English Language
description: A rhyme on two syllables, the last unstressed. “motion / ocean”.

name: Flyting
subject: English Language
description: A contest of insults, traded in verse.

name: Foil
subject: English Language
description: A character whose opposite qualities highlight another’s.

name: Frame Narrative
subject: English Language
description: A story told inside another story.

name: Flashback
subject: English Language
description: A scene that jumps back to an earlier time.

name: Foreshadowing
subject: English Language
description: A hint early on of what is to come.

name: Free verse
subject: English Language
description: Poetry with no fixed metre or rhyme scheme.

name: Hamartia
subject: English Language
description: The flaw or mistake that brings a tragic hero down.

name: Hemistich
subject: English Language
description: Half a line of verse, usually split by a pause.

name: Hendiadys
subject: English Language
description: One idea expressed as two nouns joined by “and”. “Sound and fury” for furious sound.

name: Homonym
subject: English Language
description: Words spelt and said the same with different meanings. “bat”.

name: Homophone
subject: English Language
description: Words that sound the same but are spelt differently. “there / their”.

name: Hubris
subject: English Language
description: Excessive pride, usually the thing that causes the fall.

name: Hypallage
subject: English Language
description: Swapping which word an adjective belongs to. “A sleepless night.”

name: Hyperbaton
subject: English Language
description: Words separated from the ones they belong with, for emphasis.

name: Hyperbole
subject: English Language
description: Deliberate exaggeration, not meant literally. “I’ve told you a thousand times.”

name: Hypocorism
subject: English Language
description: A pet name or affectionate diminutive.

name: Hypostatisation
subject: English Language
description: Treating an idea as though it were a real thing that can act.

name: Hypotyposis
subject: English Language
description: Description so vivid the scene seems to be in front of you.

name: Hypozeuxis
subject: English Language
description: Giving every clause its own subject and verb, for weight.

name: Idiom
subject: English Language
description: A phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from its words. “Kick the bucket.”

name: Imagery
subject: English Language
description: Language that appeals to the senses to build a picture.

name: Invective
subject: English Language
description: Abusive, attacking language.

name: Inversion
subject: English Language
description: Reversing the normal word order. “Into the valley rode the six hundred.”

name: Invocation
subject: English Language
description: Calling on a muse or a god for help, usually at the start of an epic.

name: In media res
subject: English Language
description: Beginning in the middle of the action rather than at the start.

name: Irony
subject: English Language
description: Saying one thing and meaning another, or an outcome that is the opposite of what was expected.

name: Isocolon
subject: English Language
description: Clauses of matching length and structure. “Veni, vidi, vici.”

name: Juxtaposition
subject: English Language
description: Two things placed side by side so the contrast shows.

name: Jargon
subject: English Language
description: Specialist vocabulary belonging to a trade or group.

name: Kenning
subject: English Language
description: A compound phrase standing in for a noun. “Whale-road” for the sea.

name: Light rhyme
subject: English Language
description: A rhyme where one syllable is stressed and the other is not.

name: Litotes
subject: English Language
description: Understatement made by denying the opposite. “Not bad” for good.

name: Malapropism
subject: English Language
description: The wrong word used for one that sounds like it, comically. “Dance a flamingo.”

name: Masculine rhyme
subject: English Language
description: A rhyme on a single stressed syllable. “hand / stand”.

name: Meiosis
subject: English Language
description: Belittling something by describing it as far less than it is.

name: Melodrama
subject: English Language
description: Exaggerated emotion and sensational plot, characters drawn broadly.

name: Metalepsis
subject: English Language
description: A reference so indirect it needs a second leap to follow.

name: Metaphor
subject: English Language
description: Saying one thing IS another. “Time is a thief.”

name: Meter
subject: English Language
description: The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line.

name: Metonymy
subject: English Language
description: Naming something by a thing closely linked to it. “The Crown” for the monarchy.

name: Monologue
subject: English Language
description: One character speaking at length, alone or to others.

name: Motif
subject: English Language
description: An image or idea that recurs through a work and builds meaning.

name: Mythopoeia
subject: English Language
description: Making a myth — inventing a legend rather than retelling one.

name: Neologism
subject: English Language
description: A newly invented word.

name: Nonce-word
subject: English Language
description: A word coined for one occasion and not used again.

name: Onomatopoeia
subject: English Language
description: A word that sounds like the thing it names. “Buzz”, “crash”.

name: Oxymoron
subject: English Language
description: Two contradictory words together. “Bittersweet”, “deafening silence”.

name: Palilogy
subject: English Language
description: Immediate repetition of a word for emphasis.

name: Paradox
subject: English Language
description: A statement that contradicts itself and is still true. “Less is more.”

name: Paralipsis
subject: English Language
description: Drawing attention to something by saying you will not mention it.

name: Parallelism
subject: English Language
description: Matching grammatical structure across phrases or clauses.

name: Parataxis
subject: English Language
description: Short clauses set side by side without conjunctions.

name: Parenthesis
subject: English Language
description: An aside inserted into a sentence, in brackets or dashes.

name: Paronomasia
subject: English Language
description: A pun — wordplay on words that sound alike.

name: Pathetic fallacy
subject: English Language
description: Weather or landscape reflecting a character’s mood.

name: Periphrasis
subject: English Language
description: Using more words than needed — a roundabout way of naming something.

name: Personification
subject: English Language
description: Giving human qualities to something that is not human. “The wind whispered.”

name: Platitude
subject: English Language
description: A flat, obvious remark offered as though it were wisdom.

name: Polyptoton
subject: English Language
description: Repeating a word in different forms. “With eager feeding food doth choke the feeder.”

name: Polysyndeton
subject: English Language
description: Repeating conjunctions to slow a list down. “and… and… and…”

name: Prolepsis
subject: English Language
description: Treating a future event as though it had already happened.

name: Prodiorthosis
subject: English Language
description: Warning the audience that what comes next may shock them.

name: Protagonist
subject: English Language
description: The main character, whose choices drive the story.

name: Repartee
subject: English Language
description: Quick, witty reply — conversation as a duel.

name: Rhetorical question
subject: English Language
description: A question asked for effect, not for an answer.

name: Rhyme
subject: English Language
description: Matching sounds at the ends of words or lines.

name: Rhythm
subject: English Language
description: The beat of the language — how stresses fall as it is read.

name: Satire
subject: English Language
description: Using humour and exaggeration to criticise people or institutions.

name: Sentence structure
subject: English Language
description: How a sentence is built — short and blunt, or long and layered — and what that does.

name: Setting
subject: English Language
description: Where and when a piece takes place, and the mood that creates.

name: Simile
subject: English Language
description: Comparing with “like” or “as”. “As cold as stone.”

name: Statistics
subject: English Language
description: Numbers used as evidence to make an argument harder to argue with.

name: Stichomythia
subject: English Language
description: Rapid dialogue in single alternating lines, used in argument.

name: Stream of consciousness
subject: English Language
description: Writing that follows thought as it actually runs, unordered.

name: Symbolism
subject: English Language
description: An object standing for an idea beyond itself.

name: Synaesthesia
subject: English Language
description: Describing one sense in terms of another. “A loud shirt.”

name: Syncope
subject: English Language
description: Dropping a sound from the middle of a word. “ne’er”.

name: Synecdoche
subject: English Language
description: A part standing for the whole. “All hands on deck.”

name: Tapinosis
subject: English Language
description: Language that belittles its subject.

name: Tmesis
subject: English Language
description: Splitting a word and putting something inside it. “Abso-bloody-lutely.”

name: Theme
subject: English Language
description: The underlying idea a work keeps returning to.

name: Tone
subject: English Language
description: The attitude the writing takes toward its subject.

name: Topothesia
subject: English Language
description: A description of an imaginary place.

name: Triple (Rule of Three)
subject: English Language
description: Three items together, which is the number that sounds complete. “Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.”

name: Unreliable Narrator
subject: English Language
description: A narrator whose account cannot be trusted.

name: Verisimilitude
subject: English Language
description: The appearance of being true to life.

name: Voice
subject: English Language
description: The distinct personality that comes through in the writing.

name: Zeugma
subject: English Language
description: One word governing two others, often oddly. “She took her coat and her leave.”

number of red counters : number of blue counters = 1 : 2

html:
A and B are points on a circle, centre O. BC is a tangent to the circle. AOC is a straight line. Angle ABO = x°

Find the size of angle ACB, in terms of x. Give your answer in its simplest form. Give reasons for each stage of your working.
answer: (90 − 2x)° — OA = OB are radii, so angle OAB = x° (base angles of an isosceles triangle) and angle AOB = (180 − 2x)°. AOC is straight, so angle BOC = 2x°. The tangent meets the radius at 90°, so in triangle OBC angle BCO = 180 − 90 − 2x.

html: Prove that the square of an odd number is always 1 more than a multiple of 4
answer: An odd number is 2n + 1, and (2n + 1)2 = 4n2 + 4n + 1 = 4(n2 + n) + 1, which is 1 more than a multiple of 4.

y is inversely proportional to d2. When d = 10, y = 4

d is directly proportional to x2. When x = 2, d = 24

html:

html:
A force of 70 newtons acts on an area of 20 cm2, where pressure = force ÷ area.

Helen says, “The pressure decreases by less than 20%”

Is Helen correct? You must show how you get your answer.
answer: No. The pressure starts at 70 ÷ 20 = 3.5 N/cm<sup>2</sup> and becomes 80 ÷ 30 = 2.666… N/cm<sup>2</sup>, a fall of 0.8333…, which is 23.8% of 3.5 — more than 20%, not less.

subject: Maths

Shape A is drawn on a grid with vertices (3, 10), (6, 10), (6, 7) and (3, 4).

Enlarge shape A by scale factor 1⁄3 centre (0, 1)
answer: A shape with vertices (1, 4), (2, 4), (2, 3) and (1, 2) — each point moves to one third of its distance from (0, 1), so (3, 10) → (1, 4) and (3, 4) → (1, 2)

html:
60 people were asked if they prefer to go on holiday in Britain or in Spain or in Italy.

38 of the people were male. 11 of the 32 people who said Britain were female. 8 males said Italy. 12 people said Spain.

One of the females is chosen at random. What is the probability that this female said Spain?
answer: <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>22</sub> — 22 of the 60 are female. 21 males said Britain, so of the 38 males 38 − 21 − 8 = 9 said Spain, leaving 12 − 9 = 3 females who said Spain.

Jean invests £12 000 in an account paying compound interest for 2 years.

In the first year the rate of interest is x% and at the end of the first year the value of Jean’s investment is £12 336

In the second year the rate of interest is x⁄2%

What is the value of Jean’s investment at the end of 2 years?
answer: £12 508.70 — the first year adds £336 to £12 000, so x = 2.8. The second year is 1.4%, and 12 336 × 1.014 = 12 508.704

Four sketch graphs of y against x represent four different types of proportionality. html:
A, B, C and D are points on the circumference of a circle, centre O. FDE is a tangent to the circle. Angle BDO = x° and angle BAD = y°

Show that y − x = 90. You must give a reason for each stage of your working.
answer: OB = OD because both are radii, so triangle OBD is isosceles and angle OBD = x° (base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal). The angles of triangle OBD add to 180°, so angle BOD = (180 − 2x)°. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so angle BCD = (90 − x)°. ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, so its opposite angles add to 180°: y + 90 − x = 180, giving y − x = 90

answer: He got the last term of the denominator wrong. Expanding (2 + √3)(2 − √3) ends in −√3 × √3 = −3, not +3, so the denominator is 4 − 3 = 1 and the answer is 28 − 14√3

html:
Jackson is trying to find the density, in g/cm3, of a block of wood. The block is a cuboid. He measures the length as 13.2 cm, the width as 16.0 cm and the height as 21.7 cm, each correct to the nearest mm. He measures the mass as 1970 g, correct to the nearest 5 g.

By considering bounds, work out the density of the wood. Give your answer to a suitable degree of accuracy. You must show all your working and give a reason for your final answer.
answer: 0.43 g/cm<sup>3</sup> — the mass lies between 1967.5 g and 1972.5 g and each length is within 0.05 cm, so the volume lies between 13.15 × 15.95 × 21.65 = 4540.6… and 13.25 × 16.05 × 21.75 = 4625.4… cm<sup>3</sup>. Dividing the smallest mass by the largest volume gives 0.42536… and the largest mass by the smallest volume gives 0.43438…. Both round to 0.43, so the density is 0.43 g/cm<sup>3</sup> to 2 decimal places — the bounds agree that far and no further.

When a biased 6-sided dice is thrown once, the probability that it will land on 4 is 0.65. The biased dice is thrown twice.

Write down two things that are wrong with the probability tree diagram.
answer: First, the two first-throw branches are 0.65 and 0.25, which add to 0.9 — a pair of branches must add to 1, so “not land on 4” should be 0.35. A graph shows the speed of a car, in metres per second, during the first 20 seconds of a journey. The curve rises steeply and then flattens, reading 0 at 0 s, 22 at 5 s, 28 at 10 s, 32 at 15 s and 35 m/s at 20 s.

Work out an estimate for the distance the car travelled in the first 20 seconds. Use 4 strips of equal width.
answer: 497.5 metres — the distance is the area under the graph. Four trapezia each 5 seconds wide give <sup>5</sup>⁄<sub>2</sub> × [0 + 2(22 + 28 + 32) + 35]
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html: Is your answer to part (a) an underestimate or an overestimate of the actual distance the car travelled in the first 20 seconds? Give a reason for your answer.
answer: An underestimate. The curve bends downwards, so each straight top edge cuts below the curve and every strip misses the sliver of area between the two.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html:
The nth term of a sequence is given by an2 + bn where a and b are integers. The 2nd term of the sequence is −2 and the 4th term is 12

Find the 6th term of the sequence.
answer: 42 — the two terms give 4a + 2b = −2 and 16a + 4b = 12, so a = 2 and b = −5. Then the 6th term is 2 × 36 − 5 × 6
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html:
Here are the first five terms of a different quadratic sequence: 0, 2, 6, 12, 20

Find an expression, in terms of n, for the nth term of this sequence.
answer: n2 − n, or n(n − 1) — the differences are 2, 4, 6, 8 and the second difference is 2, so the n2 coefficient is 1. Taking n2 away leaves −1, −2, −3, −4, −5, which is −n. It gives 0, 2, 6, 12, 20 back.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html:
Triangles ABD and BCD share the side BD. AB = 11.4 cm, DC = 12.5 cm, angle ABD = 86°, angle DBC = 109° and angle BCD = 34°

Work out the length of AD. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
answer: 13.1 cm — in triangle BCD the third angle BDC is 180 − 109 − 34 = 37°, and the sine rule gives BD = 12.5 × sin 34° ÷ sin 109° = 7.3927… cm. Then the cosine rule in triangle ABD: AD2 = 11.42 + 7.39272 − 2 × 11.4 × 7.3927 × cos 86°, so AD = 13.147…
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html: Show that the equation x3 + x = 7 has a solution between 1 and 2
answer: Put f(x) = x3 + x − 7. Then f(1) = 1 + 1 − 7 = −5 and f(2) = 8 + 2 − 7 = 3. The sign changes between them and the curve is unbroken, so it crosses zero somewhere between 1 and 2.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html: Show that the equation x3 + x = 7 can be rearranged to give x = ∛(7 − x)
answer: Take x from both sides: x3 = 7 − x. Then take the cube root of each side.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html: Starting with x0 = 2, use the iteration formula xn+1 = ∛(7 − xn) three times to find an estimate for a solution of x3 + x = 7
answer: 1.739 — x1 = ∛5 = 1.70997…, x2 = ∛5.29002… = 1.74241…, x3 = ∛5.25758… = 1.73885…, which is settling between 1 and 2 as part (a) said it must
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html:
Here are two right-angled triangles. The first has the side opposite angle e equal to x and the side next to it equal to 4x − 1. The second has the side opposite angle f equal to 6x + 5 and the side next to it equal to 12x + 31

Given that tan e = tan f, find the value of x. You must show all your working.
answer: x = 5⁄3 — cross-multiplying x⁄(4x − 1) = (6x + 5)⁄(12x + 31) gives 12x2 + 31x = 24x2 + 14x − 5, so 12x2 − 17x − 5 = 0 and (3x − 5)(4x + 1) = 0. The other root, −0.25, would make every side negative, so it is thrown away.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html:
50 people were asked if they speak French or German or Spanish. Of these people, 31 speak French, 2 speak French, German and Spanish, 4 speak French and Spanish but not German, 7 speak German and Spanish, 8 do not speak any of the languages, and all 10 people who speak German speak at least one other language.

Two of the 50 people are chosen at random. Work out the probability that they both only speak Spanish.
answer: <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>245</sub> — filling in the Venn diagram from the middle out: German and Spanish but not French is 7 − 2 = 5, and since no one speaks German alone, French and German but not Spanish is 10 − 5 − 2 = 3. French only is 31 − 3 − 4 − 2 = 22. That leaves 50 − 8 − 22 − 3 − 4 − 5 − 2 = 6 who speak only Spanish, so the probability is <sup>6</sup>⁄<sub>50</sub> × <sup>5</sup>⁄<sub>49</sub>
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html:
ABCD is a parallelogram. ABP and QDC are straight lines. Angle ADP = angle CBQ = 90°

Prove that triangle ADP is congruent to triangle CBQ.
answer: AD = CB, because opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal. Angle ADP = angle CBQ = 90°, which is given. P lies on AB produced, so angle DAP is angle DAB; Q lies on CD produced, so angle BCQ is angle BCD — and those are opposite angles of the parallelogram, so they are equal. Two angles and the corresponding side match, so the triangles are congruent (AAS).
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html: Explain why AQ is parallel to PC.
answer: The congruence gives AP = CQ. AP lies along AB and CQ along CD, which are parallel, so AP and QC are equal and parallel. A quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel is a parallelogram, so APCQ is one and its other pair of sides, AQ and PC, are parallel too.
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — June 2018
subject: Maths

html: Work out the value of (37 × 3−2)⁄33
answer: 9 — the powers add on top and subtract underneath: 3<sup>7 − 2 − 3</sup> = 3<sup>2</sup>
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2018
subject: Maths

html:
v2 = u2 + 2as, where u = 12, a = −3 and s = 18

Work out a value of v.
answer: 6 — v2 = 144 + 2 × (−3) × 18 = 144 − 108 = 36. (−6 is the other value.)
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2018
subject: Maths

html: Make s the subject of v2 = u2 + 2as
answer: s = (v2 − u2)⁄2a
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2018
subject: Maths

html:
A bonus of £2100 is shared by 10 people who work for a company. 40% of the bonus is shared equally between 3 managers. The rest of the bonus is shared equally between 7 salesmen.

One of the salesmen says, “If the bonus is shared equally between all 10 people I will get 25% more money.”

Is the salesman correct? You must show how you get your answer.
answer: No. 40% of £2100 is £840, so each manager gets £280 and the salesmen share £1260, which is £180 each. An equal split of all ten shares is £210, and going from 180 to 210 is a rise of 30⁄<sub>180</sub> = 16.7%, not 25%.
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2018
subject: Maths

html:
It would take 120 minutes to fill a swimming pool using water from 5 taps.

How many minutes will it take to fill the pool if only 3 of the taps are used?
answer: 200 minutes — fewer taps means longer, so 120 × <sup>5</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2018
subject: Maths

html: State one assumption you made in working out your answer to part (a).
answer: That every tap delivers water at the same steady rate.
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2018
subject: Maths

html:
A plane travels at a speed of 213 miles per hour.

Work out an estimate for the number of seconds the plane takes to travel 1 mile.
answer: 18 seconds — round 213 to 200 miles per hour. That is 200 miles in 3600 seconds, so 3600 ÷ 200 for one mile
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2018
subject: Maths

html: Is your answer to part (a) an underestimate or an overestimate? Give a reason for your answer.
answer: An overestimate. 200 is less than 213, so the estimate has the plane flying slower than it really does, which makes each mile take longer — 18 seconds against the true 16.9…
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2018
subject: Maths

html:
Solve the simultaneous equations

5x + y = 21
x − 3y = 9
answer: x = 4.5, y = −1.5 — multiplying the first equation by 3 gives 15x + 3y = 63, and adding the second gives 16x = 72. Check in the second equation: 4.5 − 3 × (−1.5) = 9
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2018
subject: Maths

html:
A square ABCD has sides of length 20 cm, with A bottom left, B bottom right, C top right and D top left. AB is the diameter of a semicircle drawn inside the square, and AC is an arc of a circle with centre B. The shaded region lies between the two.

Show that (area of shaded region)⁄(area of square) = π⁄8
answer: The arc from A to C has centre B and radius BA = BC = 20, and the angle at B is the square’s right angle, so it cuts off a quarter circle of area ¼ × π × 202 = 100π. The semicircle on AB has radius 10 and area ½ × π × 102 = 50π. The shaded region is the difference, 50π, and the square is 400, so the ratio is 50π⁄400 = π⁄8
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2018
subject: Maths
