html:
The distance-time graph for a car’s journey runs from (0 s, 0 m) up to (20 s, 360 m), then less steeply to (60 s, 560 m), then flat to 80 s.

Between which two times does the car travel at its greatest speed? Give a reason for your answer.
answer: Between 0 and 20 seconds, because that is where the graph is steepest, and on a distance-time graph the gradient IS the speed. The flat part at the end is the car not moving at all
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Work out this greatest speed.
answer: 18 m/s — the gradient of the first section: 360 m in 20 s
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
Two pie charts, drawn accurately, give information about the ages in years of people living in two towns, Adley and Bridford. The ratio of the number of people living in Adley to the number living in Bridford is given by the ratio of the AREAS of the pie charts. Measured, Adley’s radius is 5 cm against Bridford’s 4 cm, and Adley’s 0 – 19 sector is 70°.

What proportion of the total number of people living in these two towns live in Adley and are aged 0 – 19? Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
answer: 0.119, about 11.9%. Two measurements are needed, and both come off the page. The areas are in the ratio 5<sup>2</sup> : 4<sup>2</sup> = 25 : 16, so Adley holds <sup>25</sup>⁄<sub>41</sub> of the two towns’ people. Its 0 – 19 sector measures 70° of 360°. Multiply: <sup>25</sup>⁄<sub>41</sub> × <sup>70</sup>⁄<sub>360</sub> = 0.1185…. Using the radii 5 : 4 rather than their squares gives 0.132 and is the whole of the difficulty here
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
RS and ST are 2 sides of a regular 12-sided polygon. RT is a diagonal of the polygon.

Work out the size of angle STR. You must show your working.
answer: 15° — the interior angle of a regular 12-gon is (12 − 2) × 180 ÷ 12 = 150°, so angle RST = 150°. RS and ST are sides of a REGULAR polygon so they are equal, making triangle RST isosceles, and the two base angles share what is left: (180 − 150) ÷ 2
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
At the beginning of 2009, Mr Veale bought a company. The value of the company was £50 000. Each year the value of the company increased by 2%.

Calculate the value of the company at the beginning of 2017. Give your answer correct to the nearest £100
answer: £58 600 — 2009 to 2017 is 8 years, so 50 000 × 1.02<sup>8</sup> = £58 582.97, which rounds to £58 600. Counting the years off the two dates is where this goes wrong: it is 8, not 9
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
At the beginning of 2009 the value of a different company was £250 000. In 6 years the value of this company increased to £325 000. This is equivalent to an increase of x% each year.

Find the value of x. Give your answer correct to 2 significant figures.
answer: 4.5 — the value was multiplied by 325 000 ÷ 250 000 = 1.3 over the six years, so the yearly multiplier is the sixth root: 1.3<sup>1⁄6</sup> = 1.04469…, an increase of 4.469…% a year. Dividing the 30% by 6 gives 5% and is wrong, because the interest compounds
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
On the grid, shade the region that satisfies all these inequalities: y > 1, x + y < 5, y > 2x.

Label the region R.
answer: The triangle with corners (½, 1), (4, 1) and (12⁄3, 31⁄3). Draw y = 1, x + y = 5 and y = 2x, then keep what is above the first, below the second and above the third — test (1, 2) and all three hold. Every inequality here is strict, so all three lines are DASHED
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
Tracey is going to choose a main course and a dessert in a cafe. She can choose from 8 main courses and 7 desserts. Tracey says that to work out the number of different ways of choosing a main course and a dessert you add 8 and 7

Is Tracey correct? You must give a reason for your answer.
answer: No — she should multiply. Each of the 8 mains can be paired with any of the 7 desserts, so there are 8 × 7 = 56 meals. Adding would count the number of DISHES, not the number of pairs
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
12 teams play in a competition. Each team plays each other team exactly once.

Work out the total number of games played.
answer: 66 — each of the 12 teams plays the other 11, which is 12 × 11 = 132 — but that counts every game twice, once from each team’s side. So halve it. Forgetting the halving is the mistake this question is set to catch
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Solve (x − 2)2 = 3. Give your solutions correct to 3 significant figures.
answer: x = 3.73 or x = 0.268 — it is already a completed square, so take the square root of both sides and keep BOTH signs: x − 2 = ±√3 = ±1.7320…. Then add 2 to each. Expanding into a quadratic and using the formula works but is three times the effort
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
The table gives information about the heights of 150 students: 140 < h ≤ 150 — 15; 150 < h ≤ 155 — 30; 155 < h ≤ 160 — 51; 160 < h ≤ 165 — 36; 165 < h ≤ 180 — 18.

On the grid, draw a histogram for this information.
answer: Bars of frequency density = frequency ÷ class width: 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5, 30 ÷ 5 = 6, 51 ÷ 5 = 10.2, 36 ÷ 5 = 7.2, 18 ÷ 15 = 1.2. The classes are unequal, which is the whole reason a histogram is asked for — plotting the frequencies themselves makes the two wide classes look far bigger than they are
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Work out an estimate for the fraction of the students who have a height between 150 cm and 170 cm.
answer: <sup>41</sup>⁄<sub>50</sub>, that is 123 out of 150, or 0.82. The classes from 150 to 165 are whole: 30 + 51 + 36 = 117. The last class runs 165 to 180 and only the first 5 of its 15 cm are wanted, so take a third of its 18 students: 6. Assuming the 18 are spread evenly across that class is what makes this an ESTIMATE
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: At time t = 0 hours a tank is full of water. Water leaks from the tank. At the end of every hour there is 2% less water in the tank than at the start of the hour. The volume of water, in litres, at time t hours is Vt. Given that V0 = 2000 and Vt+1 = k Vt, write down the value of k.
answer: 0.98 — 2% less means 98% is left, and the multiplier for that is 0.98. The 2000 is not needed: k is the same whatever the tank holds
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
A triangle has vertices P, Q and R. The coordinates of P are (−3, −6), of Q are (1, 4) and of R are (5, −2). M is the midpoint of PQ and N is the midpoint of QR.

Prove that MN is parallel to PR. You must show each stage of your working.
answer: Parallel means EQUAL GRADIENTS, so find both. The midpoints come from averaging the coordinates: M = ((−3 + 1)⁄2, (−6 + 4)⁄2) = (−1, −1) and N = ((1 + 5)⁄2, (4 − 2)⁄2) = (3, 1). Gradient of MN = (1 − −1) ⁄ (3 − −1) = 2⁄4 = ½. Gradient of PR = (−2 − −6) ⁄ (5 − −3) = 4⁄8 = ½. Same gradient, so parallel — and the sentence saying so is a mark
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
OAC is a sector of a circle, centre O, radius 10 m. BA is the tangent to the circle at point A and BC is the tangent to the circle at point C. Angle AOC = 120°. The region between the two tangents and the arc is shaded.

Calculate the area of the shaded region. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
answer: 68.5 m2 — the shaded piece is the kite OABC with the sector cut out. A tangent meets the radius at 90°, so the kite splits into two right-angled triangles, each with a 60° angle at O: AB = 10 tan 60° = 17.32… m and each triangle is ½ × 10 × 17.32… = 86.60…, so the kite is 173.2… m2. The sector is 120⁄360 × π × 102 = 104.7… m2. Subtract
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
There are 12 counters in a bag. There is an equal number of red counters, blue counters and yellow counters in the bag. There are no other counters in the bag. 3 counters are taken at random from the bag.

Work out the probability of taking 3 red counters.
answer: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>55</sub> — equal numbers of three colours out of 12 means 4 of each. The counters are not replaced, so the bag shrinks each time: <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>12</sub> × <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>11</sub> × <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> = <sup>24</sup>⁄<sub>1320</sub>
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
The 3 counters are put back. Some more counters are now put into the bag, and there is still an equal number of red, blue and yellow counters and no others. 3 counters are taken at random from the bag.

Is it now less likely or equally likely or more likely that the 3 counters will be red? You must show how you get your answer.
answer: More likely. Try a bigger bag of the same shape — say 15 counters, 5 of each: <sup>5</sup>⁄<sub>15</sub> × <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>14</sub> × <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>13</sub> = <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>91</sub> = 0.0220, against <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>55</sub> = 0.0182. The reason is that taking counters out matters less in a big bag: each draw stays nearer <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>, and the probability climbs towards <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>27</sub>
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
The functions f and g are such that f(x) = 5x + 3 and g(x) = ax + b, where a and b are constants. g(3) = 20 and f−1(33) = g(1).

Find the value of a and the value of b.
answer: a = 7, b = −1. Each condition gives one equation. g(3) = 20 means 3a + b = 20. For the other, f−1(33) asks what input f sends to 33: 5x + 3 = 33 gives 6, so g(1) = 6 and a + b = 6. Subtracting leaves 2a = 14. Check: g(3) = 21 − 1 = 20
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: S is a geometric sequence. Given that (√x − 1), 1 and (√x + 1) are the first three terms of S, find the value of x. You must show all your working.
answer: x = 2 — in a geometric sequence each term divided by the one before gives the same ratio, so 1 ⁄ (√x − 1) = (√x + 1) ⁄ 1. Cross multiplying gives (√x − 1)(√x + 1) = 1, and that is a difference of two squares: x − 1 = 1
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Show that the 5th term of S is 7 + 5√2
answer: With x = 2 the terms start √2 − 1, 1, √2 + 1, so the common ratio is √2 + 1. The 4th term is (√2 + 1)2 = 2 + 2√2 + 1 = 3 + 2√2, and the 5th is (3 + 2√2)(√2 + 1) = 3√2 + 3 + 4 + 2√2 = 7 + 5√2. Note 2√2 × √2 = 4, not 2√2
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
The table shows information about the heights of 80 children: 130 < h ≤ 140 — 4; 140 < h ≤ 150 — 11; 150 < h ≤ 160 — 24; 160 < h ≤ 170 — 22; 170 < h ≤ 180 — 19.

Find the class interval that contains the median.
answer: 160 < h ≤ 170 — with 80 children the median sits between the 40th and 41st. Running totals are 4, 15, 39, 61, 80, so the 39th child is the last one under 160 and the 40th is in the next class. The question asks for the CLASS, not a number
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Draw a frequency polygon for the information in the table.
answer: Plot each frequency at the MIDPOINT of its class — (135, 4), (145, 11), (155, 24), (165, 22), (175, 19) — and join them with straight lines. Plotting at the class ends is the usual error, and the polygon is not closed down to the axis
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
In London, 1 litre of petrol costs 108.9p. In New York, 1 US gallon of petrol costs $2.83. 1 US gallon = 3.785 litres and £1 = $1.46

In which city is petrol better value for money, London or New York? You must show your working.
answer: New York, and by a wide margin. Bring both to the same unit and the same currency: $2.83 for 3.785 litres is $0.7477 a litre, and dividing by 1.46 gives £0.5121, which is 51.2p against London’s 108.9p. Multiplying by 1.46 instead of dividing turns dollars into nothing useful — the rate is dollars PER pound, so dollars divide
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
A gold bar has a mass of 12.5 kg. The density of gold is 19.3 g/cm3.

Work out the volume of the gold bar. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
answer: 648 cm<sup>3</sup> — the density is in grams, so convert the mass first: 12.5 kg = 12 500 g. Volume = mass ÷ density = 12 500 ÷ 19.3 = 647.66…. Forgetting the kilogram-to-gram step gives 0.648 and is the whole of the difficulty
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
There are only blue pens, green pens and red pens in a box. The ratio of the number of blue pens to the number of green pens is 2 : 5. The ratio of the number of green pens to the number of red pens is 4 : 1. There are less than 100 pens in the box.

What is the greatest possible number of red pens in the box?
answer: 15 — link the two ratios through green, which is 5 in one and 4 in the other, so scale both to 20: blue : green = 8 : 20 and green : red = 20 : 5. That makes blue : green : red = 8 : 20 : 5, which is 33 pens per set. Under 100 allows 3 sets (99 pens), so red is 3 × 5
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Find the value of the reciprocal of 1.6. Give your answer as a decimal.
answer: 0.625 — the reciprocal is 1 ÷ 1.6
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
Jess rounds a number, x, to one decimal place. The result is 9.8

Write down the error interval for x.
answer: 9.75 ≤ x < 9.85 — anything from halfway below to halfway above rounds to 9.8. The lower end is included and the upper end is not, because 9.85 itself rounds up to 9.9
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
The length of a rectangle is 7 cm longer than its width. 4 of these rectangles are arranged in a pinwheel to make an 8-sided shape with 180° rotational symmetry. The perimeter of the 8-sided shape is 70 cm.

Work out the area of the 8-sided shape.
answer: 147 cm2. Call the width w, so the length is w + 7. Walking the outline gives eight sides that pair up: two of (w + length), two of w, two of (length − w) and two of the length — which simplifies to 2w + 6 × length. So 2w + 6(w + 7) = 70, giving 8w = 28 and w = 3.5, length = 10.5. The area is just the four rectangles: 4 × 3.5 × 10.5. Nothing overlaps and there is no hole, which is why the area needs no subtraction
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Work out (13.8 × 107) × (5.4 × 10−12). Give your answer as an ordinary number.
answer: 0.0007452 — multiply the numbers and add the powers: 13.8 × 5.4 = 74.52 and 10<sup>7</sup> × 10<sup>−12</sup> = 10<sup>−5</sup>, so 74.52 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. “An ordinary number” means writing it out, not leaving it in standard form
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
When a drawing pin is dropped it can land point down or point up. The table shows the results for three people: Lucy — 31 down, 14 up; Mel — 53 down, 27 up; Tom — 16 down, 9 up.

Rachael is going to drop the drawing pin once. Whose results will give the best estimate for the probability that the drawing pin will land point up? Give a reason for your answer.
answer: Mel’s — she dropped the pin 80 times, more than Lucy’s 45 or Tom’s 25, and a relative frequency from more trials is the more reliable estimate. Nothing about the proportions themselves matters here
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Stuart is going to drop the drawing pin twice. Use all the results in the table to work out an estimate for the probability that the drawing pin will land point up the first time and point down the second time.
answer: <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> — pool every trial: 14 + 27 + 9 = 50 point up out of 45 + 80 + 25 = 150 drops, so P(up) = <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> and P(down) = <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>. The drops are independent, so multiply: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> × <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>. “All the results” is an instruction — using Mel’s alone is a different answer
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
Jack bought a new boat for £12 500. The value, £V, of Jack’s boat at the end of n years is given by V = 12 500 × (0.85)n.

At the end of how many years was the value of Jack’s boat first less than 50% of the value of the boat when it was new?
answer: 5 years — the 12 500 cancels, so the question is when 0.85n first drops below 0.5. The powers run 0.85, 0.7225, 0.6141, 0.5220, 0.4437: still above a half after 4 years, below it after 5. Trying values is the expected method here
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
A savings account pays interest at a rate of R% per year. Jack invests £5500 in the account for one year. At the end of the year, Jack pays tax on the interest at a rate of 40%. After paying tax, he gets £79.20

Work out the value of R.
answer: 2.4 — work backwards. The £79.20 is what is LEFT after 40% tax, so it is 60% of the interest: interest = 79.20 ÷ 0.6 = £132. Then R = 132 ÷ 5500 × 100. Taking 40% off the 79.20 instead of dividing by 0.6 is the trap
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
There are only blue, yellow, green and red counters in a bag. A counter is taken at random. The table gives P(blue) = 0.2, P(yellow) = 0.35 and P(green) = 0.4.

Work out the probability of getting a red counter.
answer: 0.05 — the four probabilities must add to 1, so red is 1 − (0.2 + 0.35 + 0.4)
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: What is the least possible number of counters in the bag? You must give a reason for your answer.
answer: 20. Written as fractions the probabilities are <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub>, <sup>7</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub>, <sup>8</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub> and <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub>, and every count has to be a whole number. The red counter is what fixes it: 0.05 = <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub>, so the total must be a multiple of 20, and 20 is the smallest — giving 4, 7, 8 and 1 counters
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
The cumulative frequency graph shows information about the weights of 60 potatoes. It runs from about (40 g, 2) up to (80 g, 60).

Use the graph to find an estimate for the median weight.
answer: About 57 g — the median of 60 values is read at a cumulative frequency of 30, so go across from 30, down to the axis. Readings from about 56 to 58 are acceptable
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
Jamil says, “80 − 40 = 40 so the range of the weights is 40 g.”

Is Jamil correct? You must give a reason for your answer.
answer: No. The curve starts at 40 g with a cumulative frequency of 2, which says two potatoes weigh 40 g or LESS — it does not say how much less. The graph never shows the lightest or the heaviest potato, so 40 is at best an estimate of the range and could be an underestimate
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Show that less than 25% of the potatoes have a weight greater than 65 g.
answer: Read up from 65 g to the curve: the cumulative frequency is about 49, so 60 − 49 = 11 potatoes weigh more than 65 g. 25% of 60 is 15, and 11 is less than 15 — or as a percentage, <sup>11</sup>⁄<sub>60</sub> = 18.3%. Either comparison finishes it, but the comparison itself has to be written down
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
Alan has two spinners. Each can land only on red or white. P(spinner A red) = 0.25 and P(spinner B red) = 0.6. Alan spins spinner A once and spinner B once, and does this a number of times. The number of times both spinners land on red is 24.

Work out an estimate for the number of times both spinners land on white.
answer: 48 — find how many goes there were first. P(both red) = 0.25 × 0.6 = 0.15, and 0.15 of the goes came to 24, so there were 24 ÷ 0.15 = 160 goes. P(both white) = 0.75 × 0.4 = 0.3, so 0.3 × 160. The 160 is the step that is easy to skip
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Write x2 + 6x − 7 in the form (x + a)2 + b where a and b are integers.
answer: (x + 3)2 − 16 — halve the 6 to get the 3 inside the bracket. (x + 3)2 is x2 + 6x + 9, which is 9 too big, so take 9 away as well as the 7: −16
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
Cone A and cone B are mathematically similar. The ratio of the volume of cone A to the volume of cone B is 27 : 8. The surface area of cone A is 297 cm2.

Show that the surface area of cone B is 132 cm2
answer: Volumes scale as the cube of the length ratio, so take cube roots: ∛27 : ∛8 = 3 : 2. Areas scale as the SQUARE of that, 9 : 4. So area B = 297 × <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub> = 132. Going straight from 27 : 8 to areas gives 88 and is the mistake this question exists to catch
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Show that the equation x3 + 7x − 5 = 0 has a solution between x = 0 and x = 1
answer: Substitute both ends: at x = 0 the expression is −5, and at x = 1 it is 1 + 7 − 5 = 3. It changes from negative to positive, and the graph of a cubic is continuous, so it must cross zero somewhere between. Saying “there is a sign change” is what earns the second mark
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Show that the equation x3 + 7x − 5 = 0 can be arranged to give x = 5 ⁄ (x2 + 7)
answer: Move the 5 across: x3 + 7x = 5. Both terms on the left have an x, so factorise: x(x2 + 7) = 5, and divide by the bracket
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Starting with x0 = 1, use the iteration formula xn+1 = 5 ⁄ (xn2 + 7) three times to find an estimate for the solution of x3 + 7x − 5 = 0
answer: 0.6704 (to 4 decimal places). Feed each answer back in: x1 = 5 ÷ (1 + 7) = 0.625; x2 = 5 ÷ (0.6252 + 7) = 0.676533…; x3 = 5 ÷ (0.6765332 + 7) = 0.670448…. Keep every figure on the calculator between steps; rounding as you go drifts the answer
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: By substituting your answer to part (c) into x3 + 7x − 5, comment on the accuracy of your estimate for the solution to x3 + 7x − 5 = 0
answer: Putting 0.670448 in gives 0.3013 + 4.6931 − 5 = −0.0055, which is very close to 0 — so the estimate is a good one, and being slightly negative says the true root is a little ABOVE 0.6704. The comment has to name the number; “it is accurate” on its own earns nothing
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
The petrol consumption of a car, in litres per 100 kilometres, is 100 × (number of litres of petrol used) ⁄ (number of kilometres travelled). Nathan’s car travelled 148 kilometres, correct to 3 significant figures, and used 11.8 litres of petrol, correct to 3 significant figures. Nathan says, “My car used less than 8 litres of petrol per 100 kilometres.”

Could Nathan be wrong? You must show how you get your answer.
answer: Yes, he could be. His own figures give 100 × 11.8 ÷ 148 = 7.97, just under 8 — but both are rounded. Consumption is largest when the petrol is at its upper bound and the distance at its lower: 100 × 11.85 ÷ 147.5 = 8.03, which is more than 8. So the true figure could be either side of 8 and his claim is not safe. Pairing 11.85 with 148.5 instead pushes it the wrong way and proves nothing
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
ABC and ADC are triangles sharing the side AC. In triangle ADC, AD = 11 m and angle ADC = 105°. In triangle ABC, angle ABC = 118° and angle ACB = 48°. The area of triangle ADC is 56 m2.

Work out the length of AB. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
answer: 14.4 m. Three steps, and AC is the bridge between the two triangles. First the area formula on ADC: ½ × 11 × DC × sin 105° = 56 gives DC = 10.54… m. Then the cosine rule for the side between them: AC2 = 112 + 10.542 − 2 × 11 × 10.54 × cos 105° = 292.1, so AC = 17.09… m. Finally the sine rule in ABC: AB ⁄ sin 48° = AC ⁄ sin 118°, giving 14.385…. Carry full accuracy through all three or the last figure moves
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
A speed-time graph for a train curves upwards from the origin. Read off the grid, the speed is 0 m/s at 0 s, about 2 m/s at 5 s, 5 m/s at 10 s, 10 m/s at 15 s and 18 m/s at 20 s.

Work out an estimate for the distance the train travelled in the first 20 seconds. Use 4 strips of equal width.
answer: About 130 m — the distance is the AREA under a speed-time graph, and four strips of width 5 gives four trapezia: ½ × 5 × (0 + 2) + ½ × 5 × (2 + 5) + ½ × 5 × (5 + 10) + ½ × 5 × (10 + 18) = 5 + 17.5 + 37.5 + 70. Answers from about 125 to 135 follow from slightly different readings
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Is your answer to (a) an underestimate or an overestimate of the actual distance the train travelled? Give a reason for your answer.
answer: An overestimate. The curve bends upwards, so the straight top of each trapezium lies ABOVE the curve and each strip counts a sliver of area that is not under the graph. Sketching one strip is the quickest way to see which way round it goes
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Prove algebraically that the straight line with equation x − 2y = 10 is a tangent to the circle with equation x2 + y2 = 20
answer: Substitute and show the quadratic has a REPEATED root. From the line, x = 10 + 2y, so (10 + 2y)2 + y2 = 20 gives 5y2 + 40y + 80 = 0, that is y2 + 8y + 16 = 0, which is (y + 4)2 = 0. One repeated solution y = −4 means the line meets the circle at exactly one point, (2, −4) — which is what a tangent is. Quoting the discriminant, 82 − 4 × 1 × 16 = 0, does the same job
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
A, B and C are points on the circumference of a circle, centre O. AOB is a diameter of the circle.

Prove that angle ACB is 90°. You must not use any circle theorems in your proof.
answer: Join OC. Every radius is the same length, so OA = OC = OB and both triangles OAC and OBC are isosceles. Call angle OAC = angle OCA = x and angle OBC = angle OCB = y. In triangle ABC the three angles are x, y and (x + y), which must add to 180°, so 2x + 2y = 180 and x + y = 90. Angle ACB IS x + y. The instruction rules out quoting ‘angle in a semicircle’ — this is the proof of it
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html:
OAN, OMB and APB are straight lines. AN = 2OA. M is the midpoint of OB. OA = a, OB = b and AP = kAB, where k is a scalar quantity.

Given that MPN is a straight line, find the value of k.
answer: k = 2⁄5. Write everything from O: ON = 3a (since AN is twice OA, so ON is three times it — not two), OM = ½b, and OP = a + k(b − a) = (1 − k)a + kb. Then MP = (1 − k)a + (k − ½)b and MN = 3a − ½b. MPN straight means MP = λMN, so 1 − k = 3λ and k − ½ = −½λ. The second gives λ = 1 − 2k; substituting into the first gives 1 − k = 3 − 6k and 5k = 2
name: Paper 3 (Calculator) — November 2017
subject: Maths

html: Write 500 as a product of powers of its prime factors.
answer: 2<sup>2</sup> × 5<sup>3</sup> — 500 = 4 × 125 = 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 5. “Powers of” is an instruction: the index form is what is being asked for, not the string of primes
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Work out 13⁄5 + 21⁄4. Give your answer as a mixed number.
answer: 3<sup>17</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub> — as improper fractions that is <sup>8</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub> + <sup>9</sup>⁄<sub>4</sub>, and over 20 it is <sup>32</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub> + <sup>45</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub> = <sup>77</sup>⁄<sub>20</sub>. The answer has to go back to a mixed number
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Show that 22⁄3 ÷ 6 = 4⁄9
answer: 2<sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub> is <sup>8</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>, and dividing by 6 is multiplying by <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>6</sub>: <sup>8</sup>⁄<sub>18</sub>, which cancels by 2 to <sup>4</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub>. A “show that” wants the working, not the answer — the answer is already printed
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Simplify (2−5 × 28)2. Give your answer as a power of 2
answer: 2<sup>6</sup> — multiplying powers of the same base ADDS the indices, so the bracket is 2<sup>3</sup>; raising a power to a power MULTIPLIES them, so (2<sup>3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = 2<sup>6</sup>. A negative index is still just a number to add: −5 + 8 = 3
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Work out 0.004 × 0.32
answer: 0.00128 — multiply 4 × 32 = 128, then count the decimal places: three in 0.004 and two in 0.32 makes five, so 128 becomes 0.00128
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A car factory is going to make four different car models A, B, C and D. 80 people are asked which of the four models they would be most likely to buy: A — 23, B — 15, C — 30, D — 12. The factory is going to make 40 000 cars next year.

Work out how many model B cars the factory should make next year.
answer: 7500 — 15 of the 80 people chose B, so B should be that share of the production: <sup>15</sup>⁄<sub>80</sub> × 40 000. Or scale up: 80 goes into 40 000 five hundred times, so 15 × 500
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Rizwan writes down three numbers a, b and c. a : b = 1 : 3 and b : c = 6 : 5

Find a : b : c
answer: 2 : 6 : 5 — b is in both ratios and has to match, so scale the first up until its b is 6: 1 : 3 becomes 2 : 6. Then the c comes straight from the second ratio
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Express a as a fraction of the total of the three numbers a, b and c
answer: 2⁄13 — the three parts add to 2 + 6 + 5 = 13, and a is 2 of them
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Emma writes down three numbers m, n and p, where n = 2m and p = 5n. Find m : p
answer: 1 : 10 — put everything in terms of m: n = 2m, so p = 5 × 2m = 10m. Then m : 10m
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
pressure = force ⁄ area. A storage tank exerts a force of 10 000 newtons on the ground. The base of the tank in contact with the ground is a 4 m by 2 m rectangle.

Work out the pressure on the ground due to the tank.
answer: 1250 newtons/m<sup>2</sup> — the area is 4 × 2 = 8 m<sup>2</sup>, so the pressure is 10 000 ÷ 8. Working out the area is the step the formula does not do for you
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Two numbers m and n are such that m is a multiple of 5, n is an even number, and the highest common factor (HCF) of m and n is 7

Write down a possible value for m and a possible value for n.
answer: m = 35, n = 14. An HCF of 7 means 7 divides BOTH, so m is a multiple of 5 and 7 and n is a multiple of 2 and 7. The smallest of each are 35 and 14, and their HCF really is 7 — that last check matters, because 35 and 70 would give 35
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Complete the table of values for y = 6x − x3 for x from −3 to 3. The table already gives y = 9 at x = −3, y = 4 at x = 2 and y = −9 at x = 3.
answer: −4, −5, 0 and 5 at x = −2, −1, 0 and 1. Cube first, then subtract: at x = −2 it is −12 − (−8) = −4, and at x = −1 it is −6 − (−1) = −5. The cube of a negative is negative, so subtracting it adds
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: On the grid, draw the graph of y = 6x − x3 for values of x from −3 to 3
answer: Plot (−3, 9), (−2, −4), (−1, −5), (0, 0), (1, 5), (2, 4), (3, −9) and join them with a SMOOTH curve. It has two turns, near x = ±1.4, so the curve rounds over rather than meeting in points — and it passes through the origin
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Lina spins a biased 5-sided spinner 40 times. Her results are: score 1 — 6, score 2 — 8, score 3 — 9, score 4 — 7, score 5 — 10. Lina is now going to spin the spinner another two times.

Work out an estimate for the probability that she gets a score of 5 both times.
answer: <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>16</sub>, or 0.0625 — the relative frequency of a 5 is <sup>10</sup>⁄<sub>40</sub> = 0.25, and the spins are independent, so square it. The spinner is biased, which is exactly why the estimate has to come from her results and not from <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>5</sub>
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Derek is going to spin the spinner a large number of times. Work out an estimate for the percentage of times Derek can expect to get a score of 1
answer: 15% — a 1 came up 6 times in 40, which is 0.15. “A large number of times” is the hint that the relative frequency is the best estimate available
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Shape P is the trapezium with vertices (6, 14), (15, 14), (12, 8) and (9, 8). Shape Q is the trapezium with vertices (2, 6), (5, 6), (4, 4) and (3, 4).

Describe fully the single transformation that maps shape P onto shape Q.
answer: An enlargement, scale factor 1⁄3, centre (0, 2). The shape has shrunk, so it is an enlargement with a fractional factor: P’s top edge is 9 long and Q’s is 3. Find the centre by joining matching corners and extending the lines back until they meet — (6, 14) to (2, 6) and (15, 14) to (5, 6) cross at (0, 2). “Fully” means all three: the word, the factor and the centre
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Solve the simultaneous equations 5x + 2y = 11 and 4x + 3y = 6
answer: x = 3, y = −2 — match the y terms: multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2 to give 15x + 6y = 33 and 8x + 6y = 12. Both are +6y, so subtract: 7x = 21. Then 15 + 2y = 11. Check in the equation you did not use: 12 − 6 = 6
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: p is inversely proportional to t. Complete the table of values: t = 100, 25, ?, 2 against p = 1, ?, 5, ?
answer: p = 4 when t = 25; t = 20 when p = 5; p = 50 when t = 2. Inverse proportion means the PRODUCT is constant: the first column gives pt = 100 × 1 = 100, and every other column has to make 100 too
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
The table shows the weights, in grams, of some potatoes: 50 < w ≤ 70 — 20; 70 < w ≤ 80 — 50; 80 < w ≤ 90 — 60; 90 < w ≤ 110 — 30.

On the grid, draw a histogram for this information.
answer: Bars of frequency density = frequency ÷ class width: 20 ÷ 20 = 1, 50 ÷ 10 = 5, 60 ÷ 10 = 6, 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5. The classes are unequal, which is the whole reason a histogram is asked for — the 50 and the 20 look nothing alike as bars even though the first class is the wider one
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
The diagram shows a sector of a circle of radius 18 cm with angle x° at the centre. The length of the arc is 4π cm.

Work out the value of x.
answer: 40 — the whole circumference is 2π × 18 = 36π, so the arc is 4π⁄36π = 1⁄9 of the way round. The π cancels, which is why no value of it is ever needed. Then x = 360 ÷ 9
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Prove that (2m + 1)2 − (2n − 1)2 = 4(m + n)(m − n + 1)
answer: It is a difference of two squares, so factorise rather than expand: A2 − B2 = (A + B)(A − B) gives (2m + 2n)(2m − 2n + 2). Take a 2 out of each bracket: 2(m + n) × 2(m − n + 1). Expanding both squares and re-factorising works too, and is three times the writing
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Sophia says that the result in part (a) shows that the difference of the squares of any two odd numbers must be a multiple of 4. Is Sophia correct? You must give reasons for your answer.
answer: Yes. 2m + 1 and 2n − 1 are general odd numbers — every odd number can be written in each form for some integer — so part (a) covers ANY pair of them, and the right-hand side has 4 as a factor with the rest an integer. (It is in fact always a multiple of 8, because m + n and m − n + 1 add to an odd number and so one of them is even, but a multiple of 8 is a multiple of 4 and Sophia is not wrong.)
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Work out the value of (8⁄27)4⁄3
answer: <sup>16</sup>⁄<sub>81</sub> — the bottom of the index is the root and the top is the power, and both apply to the numerator and the denominator. Cube-root first: ∛8 = 2 and ∛27 = 3, giving <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>3</sub>. Then raise that to the 4th: <sup>16</sup>⁄<sub>81</sub>. Doing the power first means finding the cube root of 4096 ⁄ 531 441
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A and B are points on a circle, centre O. DBC is the tangent to the circle at B. Angle AOB = x°.

Show that angle ABC = ½x°. You must give a reason for each stage of your working.
answer: OA = OB because both are radii, so triangle OAB is isosceles and its two base angles are equal: angle OBA = (180 − x) ÷ 2 = 90 − ½x, since angles in a triangle add to 180°. Angle OBC = 90°, because a tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at right angles. Angle ABC is what is left: 90 − (90 − ½x). The REASONS are the marks here; the arithmetic is one line
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Solve 1⁄x − 1⁄(x + 1) = 4. Give your answer in the form a ± b√2 where a and b are fractions.
answer: x = −½ ± ½√2. Combine the left side over a common denominator first: (x + 1 − x) ⁄ x(x + 1) = 1 ⁄ (x2 + x), so x2 + x = ¼ and 4x2 + 4x − 1 = 0. The formula gives (−4 ± √32) ⁄ 8, and √32 = 4√2, so it simplifies to (−1 ± √2) ⁄ 2. The demanded form is what tells you the surd will not cancel away
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Alfie has 11 cards: 3 blue, 7 green and 1 white. Alfie takes at random 2 of these cards.

Work out the probability that he takes cards of different colours.
answer: <sup>31</sup>⁄<sub>55</sub> — go the short way round: the only ways to get the SAME colour are two blues or two greens, because there is only one white. Without replacement, P(blue, blue) = <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>11</sub> × <sup>2</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> = <sup>3</sup>⁄<sub>55</sub> and P(green, green) = <sup>7</sup>⁄<sub>11</sub> × <sup>6</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub> = <sup>21</sup>⁄<sub>55</sub>. Take <sup>24</sup>⁄<sub>55</sub> from 1. Listing the six different-colour pairings instead works and is four times the arithmetic
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
The diagram shows a sketch of part of the curve with equation y = cos x°. P is a minimum point on the curve.

Write down the coordinates of P.
answer: (180, −1) — the cosine curve starts at 1 when x = 0, falls through zero at 90 and reaches its lowest point at 180. It never goes below −1
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
In triangle ABC, angle BAC = 30°, AC = 6.5 cm and BC = 10.7 cm.

Work out the value of sin ABC. Give your answer in the form m ⁄ n where m and n are integers.
answer: 65⁄214. The sine rule pairs each side with the angle OPPOSITE it: AC is opposite angle B and BC is opposite angle A, so sin B ⁄ 6.5 = sin 30° ⁄ 10.7. Since sin 30° = ½ exactly, sin B = 3.25 ⁄ 10.7, and multiplying top and bottom by 20 clears the decimals: 65⁄214. The demand for integers is the hint that the exact value of sin 30° is meant to be used rather than a calculator — this is a non-calculator paper
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Here are the first five terms of a geometric sequence: √5, 10, 20√5, 200, 400√5

Work out the next term of the sequence.
answer: 4000 — the common ratio is 10 ÷ √5 = 2√5 (rationalise, or check 20√5 ÷ 10 gives the same). So the next term is 400√5 × 2√5 = 800 × 5, because √5 × √5 = 5
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: The 4th term of a different geometric sequence is 5√2 ⁄ 4 and the 6th term is 5√2 ⁄ 8. Given that the terms of this sequence are all positive, work out the first term of this sequence. You must show all your working.
answer: 5. Two terms two apart give r2: dividing the 6th by the 4th gives 1⁄2, so r = 1 ⁄ √2 — the positive root, which is what “all positive” is there to settle. Then step back three terms from the 4th: divide by r three times, or multiply by (√2)3 = 2√2. (5√2 ⁄ 4) × 2√2 = 20 ⁄ 4
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A solid sphere of radius r and a solid cone of base radius r and height h. Volume of sphere = 4⁄3πr3; volume of cone = 1⁄3πr2h. All measurements are in cm. The volume of the sphere is equal to the volume of the cone.

Find r : h. Give your answer in its simplest form.
answer: 1 : 4 — set them equal and cancel: 4⁄3πr3 = 1⁄3πr2h loses the 1⁄3π from both sides and then an r2, leaving 4r = h. Neither π nor any actual length is ever needed
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A different solid sphere of radius r and a different solid cone of base radius r and slant height l. Surface area of sphere = 4πr2; curved area of cone = πrl. The surface area of the sphere is equal to the total surface area of the cone.

Find r : h. Give your answer in the form 1 : √n where n is an integer.
answer: 1 : √8. The word TOTAL is the whole question: the cone’s surface is the curved part πrl PLUS its circular base πr2, and the base is not in the formula given. So 4πr2 = πrl + πr2, which cancels to 3r = l. Then h comes from Pythagoras on the cone’s right-angled cross-section, h = √(l2 − r2) = √(9r2 − r2) = r√8. Leaving it as 2√2 is the same number in the wrong form
name: Paper 1 (Non-Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A scatter graph shows the amount of rainfall, in mm, against the number of hours of sunshine for each of ten English towns on the same day. The ten points are (1, 9.4), (1.6, 11), (2, 7.4), (2, 1), (3, 8), (3.4, 6), (4.4, 4), (5, 7.4), (5.4, 5) and (6, 1). One of the points is an outlier.

Write down the coordinates of this point.
answer: (2, 1) — every other point follows a falling trend, more rain meaning less sunshine. (2, 1) has almost no rain AND almost no sunshine, so it sits well away from the line the others make. (6, 1) is low too but fits the trend perfectly
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Ignoring the outlier, describe the relationship between the amount of rainfall and the number of hours of sunshine.
answer: Negative correlation: the more rainfall a town had, the fewer hours of sunshine. Naming the direction is the mark — “there is correlation” on its own says nothing
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: On the same day in another English town there were 7 hours of sunshine. Using the scatter graph, estimate the amount of rainfall in this town on this day.
answer: About 3 mm — draw a line of best fit through the nine points that are NOT the outlier, go across from 7 hours and read down. A least-squares line gives 3.2, and anything from about 2.5 to 4 follows from a sensible hand-drawn line. Including the outlier drags the line and the answer with it
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
The front elevation and the plan of a solid are shown on a centimetre grid. The front elevation is 7 squares wide: its left edge rises 5 squares, a slope falls from (0, 5) to (4, 2), a vertical step rises to (4, 3), and a second slope falls to (7, 1). The plan is a 7 by 3 rectangle with a line across it 4 squares from the left.

On the grid, draw the side elevation of the solid from the direction of the arrow.
answer: A rectangle 3 squares wide and 5 squares tall. The plan is a plain rectangle, so the solid is the front-elevation shape extruded 3 deep — the slopes run left to right, ACROSS the line of sight, so from the side they show as nothing at all. What you see is the silhouette: 3 for the depth, and 5 for the tallest the solid ever gets
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Here are the first five terms of an arithmetic sequence: 7, 13, 19, 25, 31

Find an expression, in terms of n, for the nth term of this sequence.
answer: 6n + 1 — the terms go up in 6s, so the rule starts 6n, which would give 6, 12, 18… — one less than each term every time
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: The nth term of a different sequence is 8 − 6n. Is −58 a term of this sequence? You must show how you get your answer.
answer: Yes — the 11th. Set the rule equal to the number and see whether n comes out a positive whole number: 8 − 6n = −58 gives 6n = 66 and n = 11. A fraction or a negative would have meant no
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A plan of Jason’s garden. ABCO and DEFO are rectangles, CDO is a right-angled triangle and AFO is a sector of a circle with centre O and angle AOF = 90°. AB = 11 m, BC = 7 m, ED = 7 m and FE = 9 m. Each bag of grass seed covers 14 m2 and costs £10.95

Work out how much it will cost Jason to buy all the bags of grass seed he needs.
answer: £186.15. Take the garden in four pieces, and get the missing lengths from the rectangles first: OA = BC = 7, OC = AB = 11, OF = ED = 7 and OD = FE = 9. Rectangle ABCO = 77, rectangle DEFO = 63, triangle CDO = ½ × 11 × 9 = 49.5, and the sector is a quarter circle of radius 7 = 38.48. That is 227.98 m2, needing 227.98 ÷ 14 = 16.28 bags — and bags do not come in fractions, so 17 of them at £10.95. Rounding 16.28 DOWN is the trap
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 14.5 cm, and the side of length x cm is adjacent to the angle of 53° that the hypotenuse makes with it.

Work out the value of x. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
answer: 8.73 — the 14.5 is the hypotenuse and x is next to the 53° angle, so it is cosine: x = 14.5 cos 53° = 8.726…
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Ella invests £7000 for 2 years in an account paying compound interest. In the first year the rate of interest is 3%; in the second year it is 1.5%

Work out the value of Ella’s investment at the end of 2 years.
answer: £7318.15 — each year multiplies by its own factor: 7000 × 1.03 × 1.015. The second year’s 1.5% is charged on the £7210 the first year left, not on the £7000, which is what makes it compound
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
The graph of y = x2 − 6x + 4 is drawn on a grid.

Write down the y intercept of the graph of y = x2 − 6x + 4
answer: 4 — the y-axis is x = 0, and putting 0 in leaves the constant term. It can also be read straight off the graph
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Write down the coordinates of the turning point of the graph of y = x2 − 6x + 4
answer: (3, −5) — read the lowest point off the graph. Completing the square confirms it: (x − 3)2 − 5
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Use the graph to find estimates for the roots of x2 − 6x + 4 = 0
answer: About x = 0.8 and x = 5.2 — the roots are where the curve crosses the x-axis, because that is where y = 0. The exact values are 3 ± √5 = 0.76 and 5.24, so readings near those are accepted. The question says USE THE GRAPH
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Chanda buys a necklace for £120. She sells the necklace for £135.

Work out her percentage profit.
answer: 12.5% — the profit is £15, and percentage profit is measured against what she PAID: 15 ÷ 120 × 100. Dividing by 135 gives 11.1% and is the usual slip
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Here are the equations of two straight lines: y = ½x − 6 and 6y = 3x + 7. Oscar says that these lines are parallel.

Is Oscar correct? You must give a reason for your answer.
answer: Yes. Parallel means equal GRADIENTS, so put the second into the same form: dividing 6y = 3x + 7 by 6 gives y = ½x + 7⁄6. Both have gradient ½, and the different intercepts are exactly what makes them two distinct parallel lines. Comparing 6y = 3x + 7 with the first equation as they stand compares nothing
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Aaliyah bought a car. In the first year after she bought it, its value depreciated at a rate of 23% per annum. In the second year, it depreciated at a rate of 19% per annum. At the end of the second year the car was worth £10 914.75

What was the value of the car when Aaliyah bought it?
answer: £17 500 — this runs backwards. Losing 23% leaves 77% and losing 19% leaves 81%, so the value was multiplied by 0.77 × 0.81 = 0.6237. Divide rather than multiply: 10 914.75 ÷ 0.6237. Check forwards: 17 500 × 0.77 = 13 475, and × 0.81 gives the £10 914.75 back
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
In an experiment, 60 students each completed a puzzle. A cumulative frequency graph shows the times taken. For these 60 students the least time taken was 24 seconds and the greatest was 96 seconds.

On the grid below, draw a box plot for the distribution of the times taken by the students.
answer: A box from about 42 to about 64 with the median at about 54, and whiskers out to 24 and 96. The two ends are given in words and the three middle values come off the curve: read across at cumulative frequencies of 15, 30 and 45 for the lower quartile, the median and the upper quartile. With 60 students those are the quarter points exactly
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: The number of insects in a population at the start of year n is Pn, and Pn+1 = kPn. Given that k has a constant value of 1.13, find out how many years it takes for the number of insects in the population to double. You must show how you get your answer.
answer: 6 years. The population is multiplied by 1.13 every year, so after n years it is 1.13n times what it started at, and the starting number never matters. The powers run 1.13, 1.28, 1.44, 1.63, 1.84, 2.08 — still under double after 5 years, past it after 6. Trying the powers is the expected method
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: The value of k actually increases year on year from its value of 1.13 in year 1. How does this affect your answer to part (a)?
answer: It doubles sooner — in fewer than 6 years. A bigger multiplier every year means faster growth, so the population reaches double earlier
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A and B are points on a centimetre grid. A is the point with coordinates (−7, 6) and B is the point with coordinates (8, −5).

Work out the length of AB. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
answer: 18.6 cm — the horizontal gap is 8 − (−7) = 15 and the vertical gap is 6 − (−5) = 11, so Pythagoras gives √(225 + 121) = √346 = 18.601…. Both gaps are subtractions of a negative, which is where the signs go wrong
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Using algebra, prove that 1.062̇ can be written as 114⁄225
answer: Only the 2 recurs, so multiply by the two powers of ten whose decimal parts match: 100x = 106.2222… and 1000x = 1062.2222…. Subtracting kills the recurring tail exactly: 900x = 956, so x = 956⁄900 = 239⁄225 = 114⁄225. Using x and 10x instead leaves the 06 misaligned and the tail does not cancel
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Faiza wants to estimate the number of rabbits in a park. On Monday she catches a random sample of 20 rabbits, tags each one and releases them. On Tuesday she catches a random sample of 42 rabbits, and 12 of them are tagged.

Find an estimate for the number of rabbits in the park.
answer: 70 — the proportion tagged in Tuesday’s sample should match the proportion tagged in the park: 12⁄42 = 20⁄N, so N = 20 × 42 ÷ 12. It assumes the tagged rabbits mixed back in and that nothing was born, died or moved between the two days
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Albie is studying the rabbits in a wood. One day he catches 55 rabbits and finds that 40 of them are tagged. Albie estimates there are 50 rabbits in the wood.

Explain why Albie’s estimate cannot be correct.
answer: He caught 55 rabbits, so there are at least 55 in the wood — an estimate of 50 is fewer than the number he had in his hands. No arithmetic is needed to see it
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
The shaded region shown on a grid is bounded by four straight lines: y = 6, x = −3, the line through (−2, 0) and (0, 6), and the line through (2, 0) and (−6, 4).

Find the four inequalities that define the shaded region.
answer: x ≥ −3, y ≤ 6, y ≥ 3x + 6 and x + 2y ≥ 2. Find each line first: the steep one rises 3 for every 1 across and cuts the y-axis at 6; the shallow one falls 1 for every 2 across through (2, 0), which is y = 1 − ½x. Then test a point inside, say (−2, 4), against each in turn — it is ABOVE the steep line, which is the side a reader expects to be “left of”. All four lines are solid, so none of the inequalities is strict
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
Two similar solid triangular prisms A and B. The volume of prism A is 58.806 cm3 and the volume of prism B is 1587.762 cm3. The cross section of each prism is a right-angled triangle. For prism B the base of the triangle is 8.1 cm and the area of the triangle is 43.74 cm2. The height of the triangle for prism A is h cm.

Work out the value of h.
answer: h = 3.6. Volumes scale as the CUBE of the lengths: 1587.762 ÷ 58.806 = 27, so the length scale factor is ∛27 = 3 and B is three times A. Prism B’s triangle has area 43.74 on a base of 8.1, so its height is 2 × 43.74 ÷ 8.1 = 10.8. Then divide by 3. Using 27 as the length factor is the trap
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A triangle has two sides of 11.2 cm and 4.3 cm with an angle of 118° between them.

Work out the area of the triangle. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
answer: 21.3 cm2 — the angle is between the two given sides, so area = ½ab sin C = ½ × 11.2 × 4.3 × sin 118° = 21.26…. An obtuse angle has a positive sine, so nothing changes for 118°
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Solve 6x2 + 5x − 6 = 0
answer: x = 2⁄3 or x = −3⁄2 — it factorises: 6 × −6 = −36 splits as +9 and −4, giving (3x − 2)(2x + 3) = 0. The formula gives the same two roots and is the safety net when the split is not obvious
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
ABCDEFGH is a cuboid with front face ADEF and back face BCHG. AD = 9 cm, FD = 13 cm and angle GHF = 49°.

Work out the size of angle FAH. Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.
answer: 56°. Three steps, each in a different flat face. FD is the diagonal of the front face, so Pythagoras gives the height AF = √(132 − 92) = √88 = 9.38. Angle GHF sits in the bottom face, right-angled at G, so the depth GF = 9 tan 49° = 10.35 and the bottom diagonal FH = √(92 + 10.352) = 13.72. Finally triangle AFH is right-angled at F, because AF is vertical and FH lies flat: tan FAH = 13.72 ÷ 9.38, giving 55.6°. Carry full accuracy through all three or the degree moves
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A graph gives the volume, in litres, of water in a container t seconds after the water starts to fill the container. The curve rises ever more steeply, passing about 8.2 litres at t = 15, 10.6 at t = 17.5 and 13.4 at t = 20.

Calculate an estimate for the gradient of the graph when t = 17.5. You must show how you get your answer.
answer: About 1 litre per second — draw a tangent at t = 17.5 and take the gradient from two points on it. The curve climbs from about 8.2 to about 13.4 litres between t = 15 and t = 20, which is 5.2 litres in 5 seconds. Answers from roughly 0.8 to 1.3 follow from different tangents, and the working has to show the two points used
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: Describe fully what the gradient in part (a) represents.
answer: The RATE at which the container is filling at that instant — about 1 litre of water per second, 17.5 seconds in. “Fully” wants the units and the fact that it is the rate at that moment, not an average over the whole time
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html: f(x) = x3, g(x) = 2x + 3 and h(x) = fg(x). Find h−1(x)
answer: h−1(x) = (∛x − 3) ⁄ 2. First build the composite: fg means do g FIRST and put the answer into f, so h(x) = (2x + 3)3 — not 2x3 + 3. Then invert by undoing the steps in reverse: cube root, subtract 3, halve
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A race is measured to have a distance of 10.6 km, correct to the nearest 0.1 km. Sam runs the race in a time of 31 minutes 48 seconds, correct to the nearest second. Sam’s average speed in this race is V km/hour.

By considering bounds, calculate the value of V to a suitable degree of accuracy. You must show all your working and give a reason for your answer.
answer: V = 20 km/h, to 2 significant figures. The distance lies between 10.55 and 10.65 km; the time is 1908 seconds between 1907.5 and 1908.5, which in hours is 0.52986 to 0.53014. Speed is largest with the most distance and the least time, 10.65 ÷ 0.52986 = 20.0996, and smallest the other way round, 10.55 ÷ 0.53014 = 19.9004. The two bounds agree to 2 significant figures and disagree at the third, so 20 is as far as the data can be trusted — and saying WHY is the last mark
name: Paper 2 (Calculator) — November 2022
subject: Maths

html:
A circle has equation x2 + y2 = 12.25. The point P lies on the circle and has coordinates (2.1, 2.8). The line L is the tangent to the circle at point P.

Find an equation of L. Give your answer in the form ax + by = c, where a, b and c are integers.
answer: 6x + 8y = 35. The tangent is perpendicular to the radius, and the radius OP has gradient 2.8 ÷ 2.1 = 4⁄3, so the tangent’s gradient is the negative reciprocal, −3⁄4. Through (2.1, 2.8) that is y − 2.8 = −3⁄4(x − 2.1), which tidies to 3x + 4y = 17.5 — and 17.5 is not an integer, so double everything. Check P really is on the circle: 4.41 + 7.84 = 12.25

name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — June 2025
subject: English Language
html:
Insert — Source A

20th century prose fiction · The Midwich Cuckoos by John Wyndham · an extract from near the beginning of a novel written in 1957

This extract is taken from near the beginning of a novel by John Wyndham. The story begins on the night of 26th September in the quiet village of Midwich.

From 10.17 that night, information about Midwich became episodic. Its telephones remained dead. The bus that should have passed through it failed to reach its destination, and a truck that went to look for the bus did not return. Someone in Oppley reported a house on fire in Midwich, with, apparently, nothing being done about it. The Trayne fire engine turned out – and thereafter failed to make any reports. The Trayne police station despatched a car to find out what had happened to the fire engine, and that, too, vanished into silence. Constable Gobby was sent off on his bicycle to Midwich; and no more was heard of him, either…

The early morning of the 27th was an affair of slatternly* rags soaking in a dishwater sky, with a grey light weakly filtering through. Nevertheless, in Oppley cocks crowed and other birds welcomed the dawn more melodiously. In Midwich, however, no birds sang. In Oppley, as in other places, hands were soon reaching out to silence alarm clocks, but in Midwich the clocks rattled on until they ran down. For Midwich lay entranced.

While the rest of the world began to fill the morning with clamour, Midwich slept on. Its men and women, its horses, cows and sheep; its pigs, its poultry, its larks, moles and mice all lay still. There was a pocket of silence in Midwich, broken only by the rustling of the leaves, the chiming of the church clock, and the gurgle of the River Opple as it slid over the weir beside the mill.

And while the dawn was still a poor, weak thing, an olive-green van, with the words ‘Post Office Telephones’ just discernible on it, set out from Trayne with the object of putting the rest of the world in touch with Midwich again.

In Stouch it paused at the village phone box to enquire whether Midwich had yet shown any signs of life. Midwich had not; it was still as deeply incommunicado as it had been since 10.17 the previous night. The van restarted and rattled on through the uncertainly gathering daylight.

A little out of Stouch the van swung sharply to the right and bounced along the byroad to Midwich for half a mile or so. Then it rounded a corner to encounter a situation which called for all of the driver’s presence of mind.

He had a sudden view of a fire engine, half keeled over, with its nearside wheels in the ditch, and a black saloon car which had climbed halfway up the bank on the other side a few yards further on, with a man and a bicycle lying half in the ditch behind it. He pulled hard over, attempting an S-turn which would avoid both vehicles. But before he could complete it his own van ran on to the narrow verge, bumped along for a few more yards, then ploughed to a stop, with its side in the hedge.

Half an hour later, the first bus of the day rattled round the same corner to jam itself neatly into the gap between the fire engine and the van and block the road completely.

The mail van was the first vehicle to stop without becoming involved. One of its occupants got out and walked forward to investigate the disorder. He was just approaching the rear of the stationary bus when, without any warning, he quietly folded up and dropped to the ground. The driver’s jaw fell open and he stared. Then, looking beyond his fallen companion, he saw the heads of some of the bus passengers, all quite motionless. He reversed hastily, turned and made for Oppley and the nearest telephone.

* slatternly — adjective meaning dirty or untidy

lead: The first part of Source A.

Choose four statements below which are true.

[the eight statements the paper prints]
answer:
AO1 — identify and interpret (4 marks)

One mark for each correct statement shaded, to a maximum of four. Shading more than four scores nothing for the extra ones and AQA marks only the first four shaded, so a fifth guess can cost a mark that was already earned.

name: Paper 2: Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives — June 2017
subject: English Language
lead: Source A and Source B together.
html:
You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question.

Use details from both sources. Write a summary of the differences between [what the paper asks you to compare].
answer:
AO1 — synthesise and summarise (8 marks)

  1. Level 4 — Perceptive summary (7–8 marks)
  2. Level 3 — Clear summary (5–6 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some summary (3–4 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Simple, limited summary (1–2 marks)

DIFFERENCES, and from BOTH sources. An answer that summarises one source and then the other without ever putting them against each other is Level 2 at best. This is not the language question — no marks for analysing method.

name: Paper 2: Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives — June 2017
subject: English Language
lead: Source B only.

  2. Level 3 — Clear, relevant (7–9 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some understanding and comment (4–6 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Simple, limited (1–3 marks)

Twelve marks here against eight for the same skill on Paper 1, and ONE source only. Referring to Source A wastes the time the extra four marks are for.

name: Paper 2: Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives — June 2017
subject: English Language
lead: The whole of Source A with the whole of Source B.
html:

In your answer, you could: compare their different attitudes; compare the methods they use to convey them; support your response with references to both texts.
answer:
AO3 — compare across texts (16 marks)

  1. Level 4 — Perceptive, detailed comparison (13–16 marks)
  2. Level 3 — Clear, relevant comparison (9–12 marks)
  3. Level 2 — Some comparison (5–8 marks)
  4. Level 1 — Simple, limited comparison (1–4 marks)

Attitudes AND methods, across BOTH texts. The single commonest loss is writing about the two texts one after the other: without comparison the answer cannot leave Level 2, whatever the quality of each half.

name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html:
Insert — Source A

20th Century prose fiction · The Grass is Singing by Doris Lessing · an extract from the middle of a novel published in 1950

This extract is taken from the middle of a novel, set in Southern Africa in the 1940s. Mary has recently moved from town to a farm after marrying Dick, a poor farmer.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html: And then, suddenly, the heat became intolerable. Outside in the bush the cicadas shrilled incessantly, and Mary’s head ached; her limbs were heavy and tense. She would get up and go into the bedroom, to examine her clothes, to see if there was anything she could do: any bit of embroidery, or an alteration. With nothing to do, she would wander on to the verandah* until at last her head began to swim, and she had to go back to the house to get a glass of water.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html: As time passed, the heat became an obsession. Outside, there was a rough heap of giant boulders, and she would watch the heat-waves beat up out of the hot stone, where the heat lizards, vivid red and blue and emerald, darted over the rocks like flames. Inside, she could not bear the sapping, undermining waves that beat down from the iron roof. Even the usually active dogs used to lie all day on the verandah. Mary could hear them panting softly, or whining with exasperation because of the flies. She would lock them out of the house, and in the middle of the morning she would tell a worker to carry a petrol tin full of lukewarm water into the bedroom, and, having made sure he was out of the house, she stood in a basin on the brick floor, pouring it over her. The scattering drops fell on the porous brick, which hissed with dryness.

subject: English Language
name: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing — May 2024
html:
‘When is it going to rain?’ she asked Dick.

‘Oh, not for another month yet,’ he answered easily, but looking surprised at her question. Surely she knew when the rains were likely to fall? She had been in the country longer than he had. But it seemed to her that in the town there had been no seasons, really, not as there were here. She had been out of the rhythm of cold and heat and rain. It had been hot, it had rained, the cold weather had come – yes, certainly; but it was something happening independently of her. Here, body and mind were subservient to the slow movement of the seasons; she had never in her life watched the implacable sky for signs of rain, as she did now, standing on the verandah, and screwing up her eyes at the great massed white cloud, like blocks of glittering crystal quartz sailing through the blue.

‘The water is going very quickly,’ said Dick, one day, frowning.

It was fetched twice a week from the bottom of the hill where the well was. Mary would hear shouting and yelling, as if someone were in agonised pain, and going out in front of the house, she watched the water-cart come through the trees, drawn by two slow-moving beautiful oxen, straining their hindquarters up the slope.

‘What are you using it for?’ asked Dick. She told him. His face darkened, and he looked at her in incredulous horror, as if she had committed a crime.

‘What, wasting it like that?’

‘I am not wasting it,’ she said coldly. ‘I am so hot I can’t stand it. I want to cool myself.’

Dick swallowed, trying to keep calm. ‘Listen to me,’ he said angrily, in a voice he had never before used to her. ‘Listen to me! Every time I order the water-cart to fetch water for the house, it means a driver, and two workers, and two oxen off other work for a whole morning. It costs money to fetch water. And then you go and throw it away! Why don’t you fill the bath with water and get into it, instead of wasting it and throwing it away each time?’

She was furious. This seemed the last straw. Here she was, living here uncomplainingly, suffering these hardships; and then she could not use a couple of gallons of water! She opened her mouth to shout at him, but before she could, he had become suddenly sorry because of the way he had spoken to her; and there was another of those little scenes which comforted and soothed her: he apologising, blaming himself, and she forgiving him.

* verandah — an open, roofed area along the outside of a house.
